## 30e562b4-7e14-433d-b759-3d1b85dd1bc2
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## Core Behavior

- Prioriti

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## DEVONthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

### Blog Critique

Flags tone slips, off-voice vocabulary, and clunky sentence structures, plus a logic and content gap analysis and a dependency-order (information-DAG) check that section order grounds each term/concept before a later section leans on it. No rewrites. When the draft is a Markdown file, delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat bullets are the fallback for pasted text.
**Triggers:** "critique this blog post", "review my blog draft", "blog critique", "voice check my blog", "does this blog sound like me"
**File:** `Skills/APR/blog-critique/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format)

**Purpose:** Competitive analysis frameworks (Porter's Five Forces, Blue Ocean, positioning maps) tailored for APR's Scrum/Agile training and GenAI-for-business-agility market. Writes new analyses to `APR/Analytics/`.
**Triggers:** "analyze competitors", "competitive landscape", "identify differentiation", "market positioning", "Porter's Five Forces"
**File:** `Skills/APR/competitive-landscape/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Existing APR competitive docs in `APR/Analytics/` (e.g. `genai-course-competitive-analysis.md`)

**Dependencies:** Bash access to Astro repo analytics folder, `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` for matching newsletter content

**Purpose:** Two modes for Mark's LinkedIn presence. Review mode (default) critiques draft posts against Mark's voice and LinkedIn-specific conventions (length, hooks, emoji, hashtags, external links) and delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup on a Markdown file (chat is the fallback for pasted text). Draft mode generates 2-3 complete draft-post options from a topic Mark gives or from his blog/glossary/newsletter content, built mostly by reusing his own sentences and phrasing from the source so the draft already sounds like him and he can edit rather than start blank. Covers Scrum/Agile posts, GenAI/LLM posts (skeptical-pragmatist lean), personal posts, and business announcements.
**Triggers:** "review this LinkedIn post", "critique my post", "LinkedIn style", "LinkedIn rubric", "post review", "does this post sound like me", "voice check on this post", "draft a LinkedIn post", "give me LinkedIn post ideas", "draft LinkedIn options", "LinkedIn post from this newsletter", "draft some posts on"
**File:** `Skills/APR/linkedin-style/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format); reference newsletters in `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` optional for calibration; cross-platform emoji policy in `_social-posting-conventions.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo)

### Newsletter Reading Recap
**Purpose:** Builds the "Mark's Reading Rabbit Hole" section for the newsletter — a paste-ready Markdown list of what Mark read since the last issue, linked to originals, with neutral one-line descriptions. Papers and PDFs lead; archived-without-highlights items are demoted to a short trailing list. Window defaults to "since the last newsletter" (auto-detected from the Newsletter folder). Skips any article already featured in the reading section of the last 15 issues (exclusion set derived from the newsletter files themselves, reading-section links only, URL-normalized); the window can widen further back since repeats are filtered. Read-only and print-to-chat only; never edits the newsletter file.
**Triggers:** "reading recap for the newsletter", "reading rabbit hole", "what should go in the newsletter reading list", "newsletter reading section"
**File:** `Skills/APR/newsletter-reading-recap/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Readwise CLI (preferred) or Readwise MCP; reads `Skills/Readwise/readwise-cli/SKILL.md` for command reference

### Newsletter Reviewer
**Purpose:** Reviews and critiques draft newsletters against Mark's authentic voice, tone, and style guidelines. Produces a structured critique with anti-pattern detections, terminology checks, a provisional subject-line check (filename-derived line plus any `// Subject A:` / `// Subject B:` A/B variants), and priority fixes. When the draft is a Markdown file, delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup (see criticmarkup-editing); chat critique is the fallback for pasted text.
**Triggers:** "review my newsletter", "critique this draft", "does this sound like me", "voice check", "newsletter rubric", "style check", "review my subject line", "subject line check"
**File:** `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format)

**Purpose:** Quarterly performance re-tier of the social-media reshare queue in `complete-social-media-calendar.md`. Approval gate before editing; refreshes the header with `calendar-audit --write`.
**Triggers:** "tune the reshare queue", "re-tier the calendar", "which reshares are working", "reshare queue review", "quarterly social queue update"
**File:** `Skills/APR/reshare-queue-tune/SKILL.md`

**Purpose:** Diagnose structural SEO issues on agilepainrelief.com. Five-section audit framework (Crawlability, Technical, On-Page, Content/E-E-A-T, Authority) tightened for an Astro content/blog site. Produces a prioritised findings report at `APR/Analytics/seo-audit-YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Findings only, no auto-fix.

## Writing Skills

### Criticmarkup Editing
**Purpose:** Default delivery format for feedback on Mark's Markdown writing -- annotate the file in place with CriticMarkup (comments `{>>Claude: …<<}`, additions `{++…++}`, deletions `{--…--}`, substitutions `{~~old~>new~~}`, highlights `{==…==}`), reviewed in Obsidian's Track Changes side panel. The voice rubrics decide WHAT to flag; this skill decides HOW to deliver it. Always delivers the full markup pass in one go (no section-by-section chunking; the CLAUDE.md chunked-review preference does not apply to CriticMarkup passes). Applies to all writing types including sales/marketing copy. Never rewrites Mark's prose outside a markup wrapper. Falls back to chat bullets for pasted (non-file) content.
**Triggers:** "edit this", "mark up my draft", "track changes", "use CriticMarkup", "suggest edits inline", "give me feedback on my writing"
**File:** `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Obsidian Track Changes plugin (`.obsidian/plugins/track-changes/`); read alongside the relevant voice rubric (apr-blog-critique, apr-newsletter-reviewer, apr-linkedin-style, Marketing/copy-editing, storybrand-messaging)

### Email Voice
**Purpose:** Mark's email writing voice, for a dictation tool to draft emails that sound like him. Covers shared structure, professional vs personal registers, mechanics, and a dictation correction/vocabulary list. Built from analysis of 50+ sent emails.
**Triggers:** "draft an email", "write this email in my voice", "email in my voice", "make this email sound like me", "reply to this email as me"
**File:** `Skills/Writing/email-voice/SKILL.md`

## Communication Skills

### Drafts Inbox
**Purpose:** Triages everything in the Drafts inbox (no longer keyed to a "cowork" tag), classifies each item, takes action, and archives when done so the inbox stays the unprocessed queue. For a large backlog, asks how far back to go and filters by `modificationDate`. Tasks route to `omnifocus-capture`.
**Triggers:** "check my Drafts inbox", "process my inbox", "what's in Drafts", "triage my Drafts inbox", "drafts inbox triage"
**File:** `Skills/Comms/drafts-inbox/SKILL.md`
**Dependencies:** Drafts MCP connector; `Skills/OmniFocus/capture/SKILL.md` (for task capture)

### Gmail Triage

## Adding or Changing a Skill

Skills are the source of truth; this index is generated. To add one:

1. Create `Skills/<Category>/<name>/SKILL.md` with the injected frontmatter keys (`name`, `category`, `triggered`, `triggers`, `purpose`, `dependencies`).
2. Run `python3 Skills/_gen_index.py` to rebuild this index.
3. Append a build-log entry to `Skills/_build-log.md`.

Run `python3 Skills/_gen_index.py --check` to confirm the index is in sync (used by the pre-commit hook).

content.text: This maps to the `linkedin-style` skill (draft mode). Let me read it, along with the relevant conventions.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: "linkedin-style"
3	category: "APR"
4	triggered: true
5	triggers: ["review this LinkedIn post", "critique my post", "LinkedIn style", "LinkedIn rubric", "post review", "does this post sound like me", "voice check on this post", "draft a LinkedIn post", "give me LinkedIn post ideas", "draft LinkedIn options", "LinkedIn post from this newsletter", "draft some posts on"]
6	purpose: "Two modes for Mark's LinkedIn presence. Review mode (default) critiques draft posts against Mark's voice and LinkedIn-specific conventions (length, hooks, emoji, hashtags, external links) and delivers the critique as inline CriticMarkup on a Markdown file (chat is the fallback for pasted text). Draft mode generates 2-3 complete draft-post options from a topic Mark gives or from his blog/glossary/newsletter content, built mostly by reusing his own sentences and phrasing from the source so the draft already sounds like him and he can edit rather than start blank. Covers Scrum/Agile posts, GenAI/LLM posts (skeptical-pragmatist lean), personal posts, and business announcements."
7	dependencies: ["`Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` (delivery format); reference newsletters in `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` optional for calibration; cross-platform emoji policy in `_social-posting-conventions.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo)"]
8	description: >
9	  Review draft LinkedIn posts for Mark Levison / Agile Pain Relief, or draft new post options in
10	  his voice. Use this skill whenever the user asks you to review, critique, evaluate, or give
11	  feedback on a LinkedIn post draft (Scrum, Agile, GenAI, or any other topic Mark writes about),
12	  or mentions "LinkedIn style", "LinkedIn rubric", "post review", "voice check on this post", or
13	  asks whether a LinkedIn draft sounds like them. ALSO use it when the user asks for LinkedIn post
14	  ideas or draft options -- "draft me some LinkedIn posts on X", "give me post ideas from the
15	  latest newsletter", "turn this blog post into a LinkedIn draft". Review mode produces a critique
16	  with targeted suggestions and does not rewrite Mark's existing prose; draft mode produces 2-3
17	  complete new draft options he can edit.
18	---
19	
20	# APR LinkedIn Style Reviewer
21	
22	This skill supports Mark Levison's LinkedIn presence for Agile Pain Relief in two modes.
23	
24	## Two Modes
25	
26	- **Review mode (default)** -- Mark pastes or points to a draft and you critique it against his
27	  voice and LinkedIn conventions, then surface a small number of high-impact fixes. You do NOT
28	  rewrite his prose wholesale: quote the text, name the issue, offer a tight fix. Everything from
29	  "Delivery" through "Critique Output Format" governs this mode.
30	- **Draft mode** -- Mark asks for post ideas or draft options ("draft me some posts on X", "turn
31	  the latest newsletter into a LinkedIn draft"). Here you generate 2-3 complete draft posts he can
32	  edit, built mostly by reusing his own sentences and phrasing from the source blog/glossary/
33	  newsletter rather than paraphrasing. See "Draft Mode" below.
34	
35	The voice profile, anti-patterns, topic modes, and LinkedIn conventions apply to both modes: in
36	review you flag violations, in draft you write clean so there are none. If it's ambiguous which
37	mode Mark wants, ask once.
38	
39	## Delivery: CriticMarkup by Default (review mode)
40	
41	When the draft is a Markdown file, deliver this critique as inline **CriticMarkup**
42	annotations written into the file, per `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` -- Mark reviews them
43	in Obsidian's Track Changes panel and accepts or rejects each. This rubric defines WHAT to
44	flag; CriticMarkup defines HOW to deliver it. Map each finding to a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
45	comment at the spot (add a `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution when you have a concrete fix, a
46	`{--...--}` for a cut), then post a short chat summary of the pass. Never rewrite Mark's
47	prose outside a markup wrapper. Fall back to the chat critique format below only when the
48	content is pasted into chat rather than a file.
49	
50	## How to Use This Skill (review mode)
51	
52	1. Read the draft the user provides (paste, file, or reference).
53	2. Identify the post's primary topic family (see "Topic Modes" below) so you apply the right
54	   calibration. If unclear, ask once.
55	3. Evaluate against the rubric below.
56	4. Produce a structured critique with these sections:
57	   - **Overall Impression** (2-3 sentences)
58	   - **Voice & Tone**
59	   - **Hook & Opening**
60	   - **Structure & Length**
61	   - **Anti-Pattern Detections** (quote + fix)
62	   - **Terminology & Language**
63	   - **Engagement Mechanics** (hashtags, emoji, CTA)
64	   - **Practitioner Takeaway**
65	   - **Strengths**
66	   - **Priority Fixes** (top 3-5 ranked by impact)
67	
68	Keep suggestions concrete. Quote the problem text. Show the rewritten version.
69	
70	---
71	
72	## Draft Mode: Generating Draft Options
73	
74	When Mark asks for post ideas or draft options rather than a critique, generate complete drafts he
75	can take and edit. This is the one place the skill produces prose, and it produces NEW posts from
76	scratch. That is different from editing something Mark already wrote: the no-rewrite-outside-
77	CriticMarkup rule still holds for any existing draft of his (see `criticmarkup-editing`).
78	
79	### The core principle: reuse Mark's own words
80	
81	A LinkedIn draft here is a re-cut of Mark's existing writing, not a fresh paraphrase of it. The
82	source blog, glossary entry, or newsletter is already in his voice, with his sentences, his
83	evidence, and his phrasing. Your job is to lift the strongest of those sentences and stitch them
84	into a LinkedIn-shaped post, not to reword them into new marketing copy.
85	
86	- **Quote and lightly stitch, don't paraphrase.** Pull actual sentences and phrases from the source
87	  and keep them close to verbatim. Trim, join, or reorder for flow; don't reword what already works.
88	  If the source says "we can't code review our way out of this mess", the draft says that, not
89	  "code review won't save you".
90	- **Keep his sentence structure.** His connected, full-sentence prose is the point (see "Sentence
91	  Style" in the voice profile). Do NOT chop his sentences into punchy one-line fragments to look
92	  more "LinkedIn" -- that is the main failure mode to avoid here.
93	- **Preserve his evidence exactly.** Numbers, study names, and citations carry over verbatim from
94	  the source ("1.7x more issues", the "CodeRabbit report", "19% slower"). Never round, restate, or
95	  invent them.
96	- **Only the connective framing is new.** The hook line, the transitions, and the closing question
97	  are the parts you may write fresh -- and even those should be assembled from the source's own
98	  language wherever possible.
99	
100	### Inputs
101	Always read the actual source in full before drafting. Don't draft from the title or from memory --
102	the reuse principle depends on having Mark's real sentences in front of you.
103	
104	- **A topic or angle Mark gives you** -- find the matching blog/glossary/newsletter and draw from it.
105	- **Blog posts** -- `agile-pain-relief-astro/src/content/blog/<slug>/index.mdx`.
106	- **Glossary entries** -- `agile-pain-relief-astro/src/content/glossary/<slug>/index.mdx`.
107	- **Newsletters** -- dated `.md` files, newest first:
108	  `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/email-automation/newsletters/`
109	- If Mark gives no seed, ask once which topic, post, or newsletter to draw from (or offer to pull
110	  the latest newsletter).
111	
112	### Newsletters (in scope, with two extra rules)
113	Newsletters are a first-class source for LinkedIn/social posts, the same as blog and glossary
114	content. Two rules are specific to them:
115	- **Both A/B options come from the SAME newsletter.** When the selected fragment is a newsletter,
116	  generate both options as different angles or passages from that one issue, not two different
117	  newsletters. (Blog/glossary items may draw each option from a different source; newsletters may
118	  not.)
119	- **Record the newsletter once it's used.** Log it in
120	  `social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo) under
121	  "Newsletters Used for Social", with the date used, so the same issue isn't mined twice.
122	
123	### New blog posts (launch promotion)
124	A newly published blog post isn't a one-and-done reshare. Promote it **3-4 times over ~3-4 weeks,
125	a different angle each touch** (the A/B options you draft are the first two of those angles). Record
126	each touch in the "New Post Launch Promotion" table in
127	`social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo): one row
128	per post, a date in the next free T1-T4 cell, and the angle in "Angles used". Keep the angles
129	distinct so it doesn't read as the same post reposted. Once the touches are done, the post
130	graduates to the evergreen queue for occasional reshare.
131	
132	### Process
133	1. Read the source in full. Mark the sentences and phrases that already carry the idea well -- those
134	   are your raw material.
135	2. Pick the single sharpest point per draft. Don't compress a whole piece into one post; one clear
136	   point each.
137	3. Identify the topic mode (Scrum, GenAI, personal, announcement) from "Topic Modes" below and
138	   calibrate the lean accordingly.
139	4. Build **2-3 distinct options**, each on a different angle or hook, each assembled mostly from the
140	   source's own sentences. Different options should draw on different passages, not reshuffle the
141	   same three lines.
142	5. Check each draft against the voice profile and conventions: connected full sentences (not
143	   fragments), 200-450 words when the material supports it, no emdash, no buzzwords, no LLM tells
144	   (contrast-framing, manufactured vulnerability, cringe transition questions, forced tricolons),
145	   ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM never bare "AI".
146	
147	### Output (chat)
148	For each option:
149	- **Angle**: [one line -- what makes this version distinct]
150	- **Draft**: [the full post, ready to paste and edit]
151	- **Source lines**: [the sentences or passage from the blog/glossary/newsletter it was built from,
152	  so Mark can see the reuse and trace it back]
153	
154	Close with one line inviting Mark to pick one to sharpen, which drops back into review mode.
155	
156	### Boundaries
157	- These are starting points, not finished posts. Mark rewrites in his own hand; expect him to change
158	  most of it. Don't over-polish into something that sounds finished-but-generic.
159	- Don't fabricate research, stats, or citations. Everything factual comes from the source or from
160	  Mark. If a draft wants evidence the source doesn't have, leave a `[cite?]` placeholder rather than
161	  inventing a number.
162	- Keep the skeptical-pragmatist lean on GenAI drafts: benefits acknowledged before the "but", never
163	  hype, never "intelligent".
164	- Deliver drafts in chat by default. Only write them to a file if Mark asks (per his no-unsolicited-
165	  files preference).
166	
167	---
168	
169	## Mark's Voice Profile (applies to all LinkedIn posts)
170	
171	### Core Tone
172	- Conversational yet professional. Like coworkers talking at a pub after work.
173	- First person singular for observations ("I've seen...", "In my experience...").
174	- First person plural for solutions ("We can improve...", "What if we...").
175	- Direct address to reader ("you", "your team").
176	- Contractions used naturally.
177	- Confident without arrogance. Educational. Empathetic to practitioner reality.
178	- Canadian English spelling (behaviour, colour, organisation) preferred.
179	
180	### Sentence Style -- Real Sentences, Not Punchy Fragments
181	
182	Mark writes in complete, connected sentences that flow into each other, the way he talks. He does
183	NOT write in clipped one-line fragments stacked for effect. Avoid the staccato "LinkedIn-bro"
184	cadence. This is a strong preference and applies in both modes: flag it in review, honour it in
185	draft.
186	
187	- **Counter-example (don't do this):** "And the flaws are structural. Training rewards code that
188	  compiles and passes tests." Two clipped beats dropped as separate lines for punch.
189	- **Do this instead:** join the thought into one flowing sentence with its reasoning intact, e.g.
190	  "The flaws are structural, because training rewards code that compiles and passes the tests while
191	  giving no reward for code that's easy to maintain."
192	- Let paragraphs run two to four sentences. A one-sentence paragraph is fine occasionally for a hook
193	  or a landing line, but a whole post built from them reads as manufactured, not conversational.
194	- Keep the connective tissue -- "because", "so", "and yet", "which means", the parenthetical asides.
195	  That connective tissue is what makes it sound like Mark and not an LLM.
196	
197	### Signature Patterns (SHOULD appear, when appropriate)
198	- Parenthetical asides for clarification, humour, or Scrum reminders.
199	- Self-deprecating humour, especially about estimation, being a "recovering programmer", or
200	  feeling old.
201	- Grounding abstract points in practitioner reality: "Teams I work with...", "I've seen...".
202	- Cites evidence (studies, DORA, named research) when making claims.
203	
204	### Anti-Patterns (should NOT appear)
205	
206	#### Buzzwords & Corporate Speak -- REJECT
207	- "Delve" (hard rule -- Mark never uses this word)
208	- "Unlock", "Unleash", "Elevate", "Supercharge", "Revolutionize", "Transform your..."
209	- "Game-changer", "Best-in-class", "Cutting-edge", "State-of-the-art", "Next-level"
210	- "Synergy", "Leverage" (verb), "Optimize" (vague), "Disrupt/Disruptive"
211	- "Rockstar", "Ninja", "Guru", "Badass" (applied to people)
212	- "Deep dive", "Unpack" (both overused)
213	- "Journey" (corporate metaphor), "Ecosystem", "Paradigm shift"
214	- "Move the needle", "Circle back", "Low-hanging fruit", "Boil the ocean"
215	- "Stakeholder alignment" -> "getting everyone on the same page"
216	
217	#### Punctuation & Formatting
218	- No emdash (-- ). Mark uses hyphens surrounded by spaces instead. Hard rule.
219	- Excessive exclamation points. One per post at most.
220	- Generic LLM-style openers: "Moreover", "Furthermore", "In conclusion", "It's worth noting that".
221	- Every paragraph starting the same way.
222	- Staccato fragment-stacking -- a run of clipped, one-sentence paragraphs strung together for punch.
223	  Mark writes in connected full sentences (see "Sentence Style"). A single one-line landing is fine
224	  now and then; a whole post of them is not his voice.
225	
226	#### LLM Rhetorical Tells -- REJECT
227	These are the giveaways that a post was drafted or polished by an LLM. Flag them hard.
228	
229	- **Contrast-framing overload ("not X, it's Y").** AI loves the negation-then-correction
230	  flip: "The goal isn't to use GenAI more, or less. It's to lead a team that uses it well."
231	  "Marketing isn't about selling, it's about connecting." "Success isn't luck, it's
232	  preparation." Humans don't speak in constant opposites. One earned contrast in a post is
233	  fine; a rhythm of them reads as manufactured insight. Say the positive claim directly, or
234	  back the contrast with something concrete instead of a rhetorical flip. Watch the sibling
235	  move too: "I'm not X, I'm Y" self-positioning ("I'm not there as a guru, I'm the guide who...").
236	- **The manufactured-vulnerability beat.** "I teach this for a living, I was being careful,
237	  and I still missed it." The confess-a-flaw-then-pivot-to-authority move. It signals humility
238	  while actually reasserting expertise, and readers now recognise it as a template. If Mark is
239	  sharing a real mistake, let it sit as a real mistake without the redemptive turn that
240	  converts it back into a credential.
241	- **Cringe transition questions.** "The catch?" "The kicker?" "The brutal truth?" AI treats
242	  these as engagement buttons; they read like infomercial patter ("But wait, there's more!").
243	  Cut them and let the next sentence stand on its own.
244	- **Tricolon build-ups.** "Knowing where it helps, where it quietly adds risk, and how to tell
245	  the difference." The rule-of-three cadence is a tell when every list snaps to exactly three
246	  parallel clauses. Vary the rhythm or make it two.
247	
248	#### Scrum Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
249	- "ScrumMaster" -- one word, capital S and M. Never "Scrum Master".
250	- "Sprint", "Product Backlog", "Product Owner", "Effective Scrum" -- all capitalised.
251	
252	#### AI / GenAI Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
253	- Say "GenAI" or "LLM" -- never bare "AI" when referring to generative tools. Bare "AI" is
254	  acceptable for artificial intelligence as a field.
255	- Never call LLMs "intelligent" -- they are tools, not minds.
256	- Never hype capabilities. Acknowledge limitations alongside benefits.
257	- Bottleneck framing: "Writing code was never the bottleneck."
258	
259	#### Tone Anti-Patterns
260	- Salesy or promotional ("Don't miss this amazing opportunity!").
261	- Arrogant expertise display ("As a leading expert..."). Demonstrate, don't claim.
262	- Apologetic hedging ("I think maybe perhaps...").
263	- Impersonal distance ("one might consider..."). Use "you" and "I".
264	
265	---
266	
267	## LinkedIn-Specific Conventions
268	
269	### Length
270	- 200-450 words is the default now (roughly 1,200-3,000 characters), one clear point per post. This is nearly double the old 100-250 guidance: LinkedIn reach has shifted toward longer, substantial posts, so give an idea room to breathe rather than compressing it into a few lines.
271	- Evidence: the State of the Algorithm Q1 2026 report found longer posts (toward 1,500-3,000 characters) perform well on reach. Mark's own LinkedIn data says topic matters more than length, so don't pad a thin idea to hit a count -- but don't strip a good one down to fragments either.
272	- Length should come from developed thought, not filler: a real example, the mechanism behind a claim, the practitioner consequence. Write it as full sentences and connected paragraphs, not a stack of one-liners (see "Sentence Style").
273	- Lead with the surprising data point, observation, or question. Don't bury the lead.
274	
275	### Hook & Opening
276	Strong opening patterns (pick one, don't stack):
277	- **Research hook**: "New research reality check:", "Plot twist: [study] shows..."
278	- **Provocative statement**: A claim that makes the reader stop scrolling.
279	- **Rhetorical question**: One the reader has probably wondered about.
280	- **Personal observation**: "I've been watching teams...", "Something I keep seeing..."
281	
282	Flag weak openings: generic setup ("In today's world..."), throat-clearing, or
283	context that could be cut without losing meaning.
284	
285	### Body Structure
286	- One clear point. Resist cramming multiple arguments.
287	- Perception vs. reality gaps work well (what people believe vs. what evidence shows).
288	- Lists of 2-4 items are fine; longer lists dilute the post.
289	- Connect back to what matters -- healthy teams, good software, practitioner reality.
290	- Close with a practitioner takeaway when the topic warrants it: a single line that hands the reader an action, a question, or a frame to apply. Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with one. Personal and seasonal posts usually don't need it.
291	
292	### Emoji
293	- **Cross-platform now:** emoji are used on Mastodon and Bluesky too, not just LinkedIn. For pipeline (batch) posts, the shared `_social-posting-conventions.md` in the agile-pain-relief-astro repo is the source of truth (same 1-2 rule; on Bluesky they count against the 290-char limit). The LinkedIn-specific detail below applies to organic LinkedIn posts.
294	- Strategic, understated. Up to two emoji per post is fine; more is cluttered.
295	- Opening emoji to catch attention works. A second emoji can mark a structural turn (e.g., the constructive pivot after a critique).
296	- Why they help: LinkedIn body text is uniform grey, so a well-placed emoji adds colour, breaks up the text, and pulls the eye to a key point or the CTA. That is the mechanism behind the report's emoji finding; it does not license overuse.
297	- Never emoji a vulnerability beat or a serious moment - it undercuts the weight.
298	
299	### Hashtags
300	- Minimal. Often none. When used, keep to 1-3 and make them meaningful
301	  (e.g., #EffectiveScrum for Scrum posts). Avoid hashtag salad.
302	- Evidence: the Q1 2026 report found posts with more than 3 hashtags performed 71% worse than posts with none. The algorithm already reads your keywords, so extra hashtags add little and can signal a weaker creator.
303	
304	### Calls to Action
305	- Genuine engagement requests over performative ones ("Looking for anecdotes about..."
306	  beats "What do you think? Comment below!"). Generic "What do you think?" prompts are dead -
307	  use a genuine question or a provocative statement instead.
308	
309	### Links
310	- Put links in the post body, not in the comments. "Link in the comments" is the dead pattern.
311	- Links do not tank reach. The Q1 2026 report found posts with 1-3 links got 43% higher reach, and
312	  posts with more than 3 links got 441% higher reach, because link-heavy posts read as genuinely
313	  useful resource collections. Links to agilepainrelief.com are fine when the destination is genuinely useful.
314	- A natural fit for Mark: one link to his own article plus a few to the sources he footnoted.
315	- Quality bar: every link should be something the reader actually wants, not filler.
316	
317	---
318	
319	## Topic Modes (calibrate tone to the topic)
320	
321	Posts generally fall into one of these modes. The voice is consistent; the lean differs.
322	
323	### Scrum / Agile Practice
324	- **Tone**: Educational, helpful, empathetic to struggles.
325	- **Evidence**: Experience-based, practitioner stories, anti-patterns observed in the wild.
326	- **Goal**: Help readers fix problems in their teams.
327	- **Structure**: Often a problem + misdiagnosis + what actually works.
328	- **Hashtags**: Regular (e.g., #EffectiveScrum).
329	
330	### AI / GenAI / LLMs in Software and Scrum
331	- **Tone**: Skeptical pragmatist -- not anti-AI, not hype. Measured, analytical.
332	- **Evidence**: Research-and-data-based (e.g., the 19%/20% perception-gap study, DORA rollback
333	  signals). Cite specifics when possible.
334	- **Goal**: Question assumptions; surface hidden costs; ground hype in evidence.
335	- **Structure**: Provocative claim + counter-evidence + implication. "Hidden costs nobody talks
336	  about" framing works well. Always connect back to Scrum values (collaboration, human judgement,
337	  context over speed) when relevant.
338	- **Hashtags**: Minimal, sometimes none.
339	- **Watch for**: Drift into dismissive or mocking territory. Mark's position is "I'm not against
340	  GenAI, but let's be realistic." Acknowledge potential benefits before the "but".
341	
342	### Personal / Travel / Seasonal
343	- **Tone**: Warm, conversational, light. Pub-with-coworkers voice at its purest.
344	- **Evidence**: Not required; this is connective tissue.
345	- **Goal**: Build relationship with the audience.
346	- **Watch for**: Too-long personal posts that lose their thread. Brevity is kindness.
347	
348	### Workshop / Training / Business Announcements
349	- **Tone**: Direct, low-key. Inform, don't sell.
350	- **Watch for**: Salesy language, exclamation marks, "amazing opportunity" energy.
351	
352	If a post spans modes (common for AI-meets-Scrum posts), apply both rubrics.
353	
354	---
355	
356	## Critique Output Format
357	
358	Structure the response like this:
359	
360	### Overall Impression
361	[2-3 sentences: Does this land? What's the main issue?]
362	
363	### Voice & Tone
364	[Does this sound like Mark? Where does it, where doesn't it?]
365	
366	### Hook & Opening
367	[Is the first line doing enough work? Specific feedback.]
368	
369	### Structure & Length
370	[Length check, one-clear-point check, flow.]
371	
372	### Anti-Pattern Detections
373	For each:
374	> **Found**: "[exact quote]"
375	> **Issue**: [which anti-pattern, or why this grates]
376	> **Suggested fix**: "[rewritten phrase in Mark's voice]"
377	
378	### Terminology & Language
379	[Flag issues only: ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM usage, capitalisation, buzzwords, emdash. If the draft gets all of these right, omit this section - Mark knows his own rules and doesn't need praise for following them.]
380	
381	### Engagement Mechanics
382	[Emoji count and use, hashtag choice, CTA quality.]
383	
384	### Practitioner Takeaway
385	[Does the post hand the reader something they can do, think about, or test in their own work? Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with a closing line that gives the reader an action or a frame to apply. Not every post needs one - personal and seasonal posts rarely do - so flag only when one would clearly help, and don't force one where it doesn't fit.]
386	
387	### Strengths
388	[Specific phrases or moves that nail the voice. Be concrete.]
389	
390	### Priority Fixes
391	[Top 3-5 changes ranked by impact, with brief rationale. These should be the improvements
392	Mark would actually make before posting.]
393	
394	---
395	
396	## Reference Material
397	
398	- `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` -- any newsletter file demonstrates Mark's voice at length.
399	  Good calibration if a draft feels off and you want to recalibrate before critiquing.
400	- `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md` -- the longer-form sibling of this skill. Voice profile
401	  and anti-pattern list overlap; this skill is the LinkedIn-shaped subset.
402	- `OutsideContent/Generated/State of the LinkedIn Algorithm Q1 2026 - Report and Call Notes.md` --
403	  the evidence behind the length, links, hashtag, and emoji guidance here (Q1 2026 algorithm data plus
404	  Mike Schmitz's commentary). Read it if you want the numbers or to re-check a convention.
405	
406	---
407	
408	## Important Notes
409	
410	- Mark does all his own writing. This skill helps him sharpen drafts, not replace them.
411	- The goal is to help Mark sound more like himself. His quirks, self-deprecation, and
412	  practitioner-grounded examples are features, not bugs.
413	- When in doubt, lean toward "a knowledgeable friend at a pub" over "a consultant on a panel".
414	- Mark's LinkedIn audience is ScrumMasters, Agile Coaches, Product Owners, managers, and
415	  adjacent practitioners. They often know what to do but lack the influence to change it.
416	  Empathy for that tension matters.
417

# APR LinkedIn Style Reviewer

This skill supports Mark Levison's LinkedIn presence for Agile Pain Relief in two modes.

## Two Modes

- **Review mode (default)** -- Mark pastes or points to a draft and you critique it against his
  voice and LinkedIn conventions, then surface a small number of high-impact fixes. You do NOT
  rewrite his prose wholesale: quote the text, name the issue, offer a tight fix. Everything from
  "Delivery" through "Critique Output Format" governs this mode.
- **Draft mode** -- Mark asks for post ideas or draft options ("draft me some posts on X", "turn
  the latest newsletter into a LinkedIn draft"). Here you generate 2-3 complete draft posts he can
  edit, built mostly by reusing his own sentences and phrasing from the source blog/glossary/
  newsletter rather than paraphrasing. See "Draft Mode" below.

The voice profile, anti-patterns, topic modes, and LinkedIn conventions apply to both modes: in
review you flag violations, in draft you write clean so there are none. If it's ambiguous which
mode Mark wants, ask once.

## Delivery: CriticMarkup by Default (review mode)

When the draft is a Markdown file, deliver this critique as inline **CriticMarkup**
annotations written into the file, per `Skills/Writing/criticmarkup-editing/SKILL.md` -- Mark reviews them
in Obsidian's Track Changes panel and accepts or rejects each. This rubric defines WHAT to
flag; CriticMarkup defines HOW to deliver it. Map each finding to a `{>>Claude: ...<<}`
comment at the spot (add a `{~~old~>new~~}` substitution when you have a concrete fix, a
`{--...--}` for a cut), then post a short chat summary of the pass. Never rewrite Mark's
prose outside a markup wrapper. Fall back to the chat critique format below only when the
content is pasted into chat rather than a file.

## How to Use This Skill (review mode)

1. Read the draft the user provides (paste, file, or reference).
2. Identify the post's primary topic family (see "Topic Modes" below) so you apply the right
   calibration. If unclear, ask once.
3. Evaluate against the rubric below.
4. Produce a structured critique with these sections:
   - **Overall Impression** (2-3 sentences)
   - **Voice & Tone**
   - **Hook & Opening**
   - **Structure & Length**
   - **Anti-Pattern Detections** (quote + fix)
   - **Terminology & Language**
   - **Engagement Mechanics** (hashtags, emoji, CTA)
   - **Practitioner Takeaway**
   - **Strengths**
   - **Priority Fixes** (top 3-5 ranked by impact)

Keep suggestions concrete. Quote the problem text. Show the rewritten version.

---

## Draft Mode: Generating Draft Options

When Mark asks for post ideas or draft options rather than a critique, generate complete drafts he
can take and edit. This is the one place the skill produces prose, and it produces NEW posts from
scratch. That is different from editing something Mark already wrote: the no-rewrite-outside-
CriticMarkup rule still holds for any existing draft of his (see `criticmarkup-editing`).

### The core principle: reuse Mark's own words

A LinkedIn draft here is a re-cut of Mark's existing writing, not a fresh paraphrase of it. The
source blog, glossary entry, or newsletter is already in his voice, with his sentences, his
evidence, and his phrasing. Your job is to lift the strongest of those sentences and stitch them
into a LinkedIn-shaped post, not to reword them into new marketing copy.

- **Quote and lightly stitch, don't paraphrase.** Pull actual sentences and phrases from the source
  and keep them close to verbatim. Trim, join, or reorder for flow; don't reword what already works.
  If the source says "we can't code review our way out of this mess", the draft says that, not
  "code review won't save you".
- **Keep his sentence structure.** His connected, full-sentence prose is the point (see "Sentence
  Style" in the voice profile). Do NOT chop his sentences into punchy one-line fragments to look
  more "LinkedIn" -- that is the main failure mode to avoid here.
- **Preserve his evidence exactly.** Numbers, study names, and citations carry over verbatim from
  the source ("1.7x more issues", the "CodeRabbit report", "19% slower"). Never round, restate, or
  invent them.
- **Only the connective framing is new.** The hook line, the transitions, and the closing question
  are the parts you may write fresh -- and even those should be assembled from the source's own
  language wherever possible.

### Inputs
Always read the actual source in full before drafting. Don't draft from the title or from memory --
the reuse principle depends on having Mark's real sentences in front of you.

- **A topic or angle Mark gives you** -- find the matching blog/glossary/newsletter and draw from it.
- **Blog posts** -- `agile-pain-relief-astro/src/content/blog/<slug>/index.mdx`.
- **Glossary entries** -- `agile-pain-relief-astro/src/content/glossary/<slug>/index.mdx`.
- **Newsletters** -- dated `.md` files, newest first:
  `/Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/APR/agile-pain-relief-astro/email-automation/newsletters/`
- If Mark gives no seed, ask once which topic, post, or newsletter to draw from (or offer to pull
  the latest newsletter).

### Newsletters (in scope, with two extra rules)
Newsletters are a first-class source for LinkedIn/social posts, the same as blog and glossary
content. Two rules are specific to them:
- **Both A/B options come from the SAME newsletter.** When the selected fragment is a newsletter,
  generate both options as different angles or passages from that one issue, not two different
  newsletters. (Blog/glossary items may draw each option from a different source; newsletters may
  not.)
- **Record the newsletter once it's used.** Log it in
  `social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo) under
  "Newsletters Used for Social", with the date used, so the same issue isn't mined twice.

### New blog posts (launch promotion)
A newly published blog post isn't a one-and-done reshare. Promote it **3-4 times over ~3-4 weeks,
a different angle each touch** (the A/B options you draft are the first two of those angles). Record
each touch in the "New Post Launch Promotion" table in
`social-media/planning/complete-social-media-calendar.md` (agile-pain-relief-astro repo): one row
per post, a date in the next free T1-T4 cell, and the angle in "Angles used". Keep the angles
distinct so it doesn't read as the same post reposted. Once the touches are done, the post
graduates to the evergreen queue for occasional reshare.

### Process
1. Read the source in full. Mark the sentences and phrases that already carry the idea well -- those
   are your raw material.
2. Pick the single sharpest point per draft. Don't compress a whole piece into one post; one clear
   point each.
3. Identify the topic mode (Scrum, GenAI, personal, announcement) from "Topic Modes" below and
   calibrate the lean accordingly.
4. Build **2-3 distinct options**, each on a different angle or hook, each assembled mostly from the
   source's own sentences. Different options should draw on different passages, not reshuffle the
   same three lines.
5. Check each draft against the voice profile and conventions: connected full sentences (not
   fragments), 200-450 words when the material supports it, no emdash, no buzzwords, no LLM tells
   (contrast-framing, manufactured vulnerability, cringe transition questions, forced tricolons),
   ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM never bare "AI".

### Output (chat)
For each option:
- **Angle**: [one line -- what makes this version distinct]
- **Draft**: [the full post, ready to paste and edit]
- **Source lines**: [the sentences or passage from the blog/glossary/newsletter it was built from,
  so Mark can see the reuse and trace it back]

Close with one line inviting Mark to pick one to sharpen, which drops back into review mode.

### Boundaries
- These are starting points, not finished posts. Mark rewrites in his own hand; expect him to change
  most of it. Don't over-polish into something that sounds finished-but-generic.
- Don't fabricate research, stats, or citations. Everything factual comes from the source or from
  Mark. If a draft wants evidence the source doesn't have, leave a `[cite?]` placeholder rather than
  inventing a number.
- Keep the skeptical-pragmatist lean on GenAI drafts: benefits acknowledged before the "but", never
  hype, never "intelligent".
- Deliver drafts in chat by default. Only write them to a file if Mark asks (per his no-unsolicited-
  files preference).

---

## Mark's Voice Profile (applies to all LinkedIn posts)

### Core Tone
- Conversational yet professional. Like coworkers talking at a pub after work.
- First person singular for observations ("I've seen...", "In my experience...").
- First person plural for solutions ("We can improve...", "What if we...").
- Direct address to reader ("you", "your team").
- Contractions used naturally.
- Confident without arrogance. Educational. Empathetic to practitioner reality.
- Canadian English spelling (behaviour, colour, organisation) preferred.

### Sentence Style -- Real Sentences, Not Punchy Fragments

Mark writes in complete, connected sentences that flow into each other, the way he talks. He does
NOT write in clipped one-line fragments stacked for effect. Avoid the staccato "LinkedIn-bro"
cadence. This is a strong preference and applies in both modes: flag it in review, honour it in
draft.

- **Counter-example (don't do this):** "And the flaws are structural. Training rewards code that
  compiles and passes tests." Two clipped beats dropped as separate lines for punch.
- **Do this instead:** join the thought into one flowing sentence with its reasoning intact, e.g.
  "The flaws are structural, because training rewards code that compiles and passes the tests while
  giving no reward for code that's easy to maintain."
- Let paragraphs run two to four sentences. A one-sentence paragraph is fine occasionally for a hook
  or a landing line, but a whole post built from them reads as manufactured, not conversational.
- Keep the connective tissue -- "because", "so", "and yet", "which means", the parenthetical asides.
  That connective tissue is what makes it sound like Mark and not an LLM.

### Signature Patterns (SHOULD appear, when appropriate)
- Parenthetical asides for clarification, humour, or Scrum reminders.
- Self-deprecating humour, especially about estimation, being a "recovering programmer", or
  feeling old.
- Grounding abstract points in practitioner reality: "Teams I work with...", "I've seen...".
- Cites evidence (studies, DORA, named research) when making claims.

### Anti-Patterns (should NOT appear)

#### Buzzwords & Corporate Speak -- REJECT
- "Delve" (hard rule -- Mark never uses this word)
- "Unlock", "Unleash", "Elevate", "Supercharge", "Revolutionize", "Transform your..."
- "Game-changer", "Best-in-class", "Cutting-edge", "State-of-the-art", "Next-level"
- "Synergy", "Leverage" (verb), "Optimize" (vague), "Disrupt/Disruptive"
- "Rockstar", "Ninja", "Guru", "Badass" (applied to people)
- "Deep dive", "Unpack" (both overused)
- "Journey" (corporate metaphor), "Ecosystem", "Paradigm shift"
- "Move the needle", "Circle back", "Low-hanging fruit", "Boil the ocean"
- "Stakeholder alignment" -> "getting everyone on the same page"

#### Punctuation & Formatting
- No emdash (-- ). Mark uses hyphens surrounded by spaces instead. Hard rule.
- Excessive exclamation points. One per post at most.
- Generic LLM-style openers: "Moreover", "Furthermore", "In conclusion", "It's worth noting that".
- Every paragraph starting the same way.
- Staccato fragment-stacking -- a run of clipped, one-sentence paragraphs strung together for punch.
  Mark writes in connected full sentences (see "Sentence Style"). A single one-line landing is fine
  now and then; a whole post of them is not his voice.

#### LLM Rhetorical Tells -- REJECT
These are the giveaways that a post was drafted or polished by an LLM. Flag them hard.

- **Contrast-framing overload ("not X, it's Y").** AI loves the negation-then-correction
  flip: "The goal isn't to use GenAI more, or less. It's to lead a team that uses it well."
  "Marketing isn't about selling, it's about connecting." "Success isn't luck, it's
  preparation." Humans don't speak in constant opposites. One earned contrast in a post is
  fine; a rhythm of them reads as manufactured insight. Say the positive claim directly, or
  back the contrast with something concrete instead of a rhetorical flip. Watch the sibling
  move too: "I'm not X, I'm Y" self-positioning ("I'm not there as a guru, I'm the guide who...").
- **The manufactured-vulnerability beat.** "I teach this for a living, I was being careful,
  and I still missed it." The confess-a-flaw-then-pivot-to-authority move. It signals humility
  while actually reasserting expertise, and readers now recognise it as a template. If Mark is
  sharing a real mistake, let it sit as a real mistake without the redemptive turn that
  converts it back into a credential.
- **Cringe transition questions.** "The catch?" "The kicker?" "The brutal truth?" AI treats
  these as engagement buttons; they read like infomercial patter ("But wait, there's more!").
  Cut them and let the next sentence stand on its own.
- **Tricolon build-ups.** "Knowing where it helps, where it quietly adds risk, and how to tell
  the difference." The rule-of-three cadence is a tell when every list snaps to exactly three
  parallel clauses. Vary the rhythm or make it two.

#### Scrum Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
- "ScrumMaster" -- one word, capital S and M. Never "Scrum Master".
- "Sprint", "Product Backlog", "Product Owner", "Effective Scrum" -- all capitalised.

#### AI / GenAI Terminology -- USE THESE RULES
- Say "GenAI" or "LLM" -- never bare "AI" when referring to generative tools. Bare "AI" is
  acceptable for artificial intelligence as a field.
- Never call LLMs "intelligent" -- they are tools, not minds.
- Never hype capabilities. Acknowledge limitations alongside benefits.
- Bottleneck framing: "Writing code was never the bottleneck."

#### Tone Anti-Patterns
- Salesy or promotional ("Don't miss this amazing opportunity!").
- Arrogant expertise display ("As a leading expert..."). Demonstrate, don't claim.
- Apologetic hedging ("I think maybe perhaps...").
- Impersonal distance ("one might consider..."). Use "you" and "I".

---

## LinkedIn-Specific Conventions

### Length
- 200-450 words is the default now (roughly 1,200-3,000 characters), one clear point per post. This is nearly double the old 100-250 guidance: LinkedIn reach has shifted toward longer, substantial posts, so give an idea room to breathe rather than compressing it into a few lines.
- Evidence: the State of the Algorithm Q1 2026 report found longer posts (toward 1,500-3,000 characters) perform well on reach. Mark's own LinkedIn data says topic matters more than length, so don't pad a thin idea to hit a count -- but don't strip a good one down to fragments either.
- Length should come from developed thought, not filler: a real example, the mechanism behind a claim, the practitioner consequence. Write it as full sentences and connected paragraphs, not a stack of one-liners (see "Sentence Style").
- Lead with the surprising data point, observation, or question. Don't bury the lead.

### Hook & Opening
Strong opening patterns (pick one, don't stack):
- **Research hook**: "New research reality check:", "Plot twist: [study] shows..."
- **Provocative statement**: A claim that makes the reader stop scrolling.
- **Rhetorical question**: One the reader has probably wondered about.
- **Personal observation**: "I've been watching teams...", "Something I keep seeing..."

Flag weak openings: generic setup ("In today's world..."), throat-clearing, or
context that could be cut without losing meaning.

### Body Structure
- One clear point. Resist cramming multiple arguments.
- Perception vs. reality gaps work well (what people believe vs. what evidence shows).
- Lists of 2-4 items are fine; longer lists dilute the post.
- Connect back to what matters -- healthy teams, good software, practitioner reality.
- Close with a practitioner takeaway when the topic warrants it: a single line that hands the reader an action, a question, or a frame to apply. Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with one. Personal and seasonal posts usually don't need it.

### Emoji
- **Cross-platform now:** emoji are used on Mastodon and Bluesky too, not just LinkedIn. For pipeline (batch) posts, the shared `_social-posting-conventions.md` in the agile-pain-relief-astro repo is the source of truth (same 1-2 rule; on Bluesky they count against the 290-char limit). The LinkedIn-specific detail below applies to organic LinkedIn posts.
- Strategic, understated. Up to two emoji per post is fine; more is cluttered.
- Opening emoji to catch attention works. A second emoji can mark a structural turn (e.g., the constructive pivot after a critique).
- Why they help: LinkedIn body text is uniform grey, so a well-placed emoji adds colour, breaks up the text, and pulls the eye to a key point or the CTA. That is the mechanism behind the report's emoji finding; it does not license overuse.
- Never emoji a vulnerability beat or a serious moment - it undercuts the weight.

### Hashtags
- Minimal. Often none. When used, keep to 1-3 and make them meaningful
  (e.g., #EffectiveScrum for Scrum posts). Avoid hashtag salad.
- Evidence: the Q1 2026 report found posts with more than 3 hashtags performed 71% worse than posts with none. The algorithm already reads your keywords, so extra hashtags add little and can signal a weaker creator.

### Calls to Action
- Genuine engagement requests over performative ones ("Looking for anecdotes about..."
  beats "What do you think? Comment below!"). Generic "What do you think?" prompts are dead -
  use a genuine question or a provocative statement instead.

### Links
- Put links in the post body, not in the comments. "Link in the comments" is the dead pattern.
- Links do not tank reach. The Q1 2026 report found posts with 1-3 links got 43% higher reach, and
  posts with more than 3 links got 441% higher reach, because link-heavy posts read as genuinely
  useful resource collections. Links to agilepainrelief.com are fine when the destination is genuinely useful.
- A natural fit for Mark: one link to his own article plus a few to the sources he footnoted.
- Quality bar: every link should be something the reader actually wants, not filler.

---

## Topic Modes (calibrate tone to the topic)

Posts generally fall into one of these modes. The voice is consistent; the lean differs.

### Scrum / Agile Practice
- **Tone**: Educational, helpful, empathetic to struggles.
- **Evidence**: Experience-based, practitioner stories, anti-patterns observed in the wild.
- **Goal**: Help readers fix problems in their teams.
- **Structure**: Often a problem + misdiagnosis + what actually works.
- **Hashtags**: Regular (e.g., #EffectiveScrum).

### AI / GenAI / LLMs in Software and Scrum
- **Tone**: Skeptical pragmatist -- not anti-AI, not hype. Measured, analytical.
- **Evidence**: Research-and-data-based (e.g., the 19%/20% perception-gap study, DORA rollback
  signals). Cite specifics when possible.
- **Goal**: Question assumptions; surface hidden costs; ground hype in evidence.
- **Structure**: Provocative claim + counter-evidence + implication. "Hidden costs nobody talks
  about" framing works well. Always connect back to Scrum values (collaboration, human judgement,
  context over speed) when relevant.
- **Hashtags**: Minimal, sometimes none.
- **Watch for**: Drift into dismissive or mocking territory. Mark's position is "I'm not against
  GenAI, but let's be realistic." Acknowledge potential benefits before the "but".

### Personal / Travel / Seasonal
- **Tone**: Warm, conversational, light. Pub-with-coworkers voice at its purest.
- **Evidence**: Not required; this is connective tissue.
- **Goal**: Build relationship with the audience.
- **Watch for**: Too-long personal posts that lose their thread. Brevity is kindness.

### Workshop / Training / Business Announcements
- **Tone**: Direct, low-key. Inform, don't sell.
- **Watch for**: Salesy language, exclamation marks, "amazing opportunity" energy.

If a post spans modes (common for AI-meets-Scrum posts), apply both rubrics.

---

## Critique Output Format

Structure the response like this:

### Overall Impression
[2-3 sentences: Does this land? What's the main issue?]

### Voice & Tone
[Does this sound like Mark? Where does it, where doesn't it?]

### Hook & Opening
[Is the first line doing enough work? Specific feedback.]

### Structure & Length
[Length check, one-clear-point check, flow.]

### Anti-Pattern Detections
For each:
> **Found**: "[exact quote]"
> **Issue**: [which anti-pattern, or why this grates]
> **Suggested fix**: "[rewritten phrase in Mark's voice]"

### Terminology & Language
[Flag issues only: ScrumMaster spelling, GenAI/LLM usage, capitalisation, buzzwords, emdash. If the draft gets all of these right, omit this section - Mark knows his own rules and doesn't need praise for following them.]

### Engagement Mechanics
[Emoji count and use, hashtag choice, CTA quality.]

### Practitioner Takeaway
[Does the post hand the reader something they can do, think about, or test in their own work? Scrum and GenAI posts land harder with a closing line that gives the reader an action or a frame to apply. Not every post needs one - personal and seasonal posts rarely do - so flag only when one would clearly help, and don't force one where it doesn't fit.]

### Strengths
[Specific phrases or moves that nail the voice. Be concrete.]

### Priority Fixes
[Top 3-5 changes ranked by impact, with brief rationale. These should be the improvements
Mark would actually make before posting.]

---

## Reference Material

- `APR/Efforts/Newsletter/` -- any newsletter file demonstrates Mark's voice at length.
  Good calibration if a draft feels off and you want to recalibrate before critiquing.
- `Skills/APR/newsletter-reviewer/SKILL.md` -- the longer-form sibling of this skill. Voice profile
  and anti-pattern list overlap; this skill is the LinkedIn-shaped subset.
- `OutsideContent/Generated/State of the LinkedIn Algorithm Q1 2026 - Report and Call Notes.md` --
  the evidence behind the length, links, hashtag, and emoji guidance here (Q1 2026 algorithm data plus
  Mike Schmitz's commentary). Read it if you want the numbers or to re-check a convention.

---

## Important Notes

- Mark does all his own writing. This skill helps him sharpen drafts, not replace them.
- The goal is to help Mark sound more like himself. His quirks, self-deprecation, and
  practitioner-grounded examples are features, not bugs.
- When in doubt, lean toward "a knowledgeable friend at a pub" over "a consultant on a panel".
- Mark's LinkedIn audience is ScrumMasters, Agile Coaches, Product Owners, managers, and
  adjacent practitioners. They often know what to do but lack the influence to change it.
  Empathy for that tension matters.

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. 2	
3	Working draft, rebuilt under the updated linkedin-style rules: each draft is a re-cut of your own sentences from the source blog/glossary/newsletter (lifted close to verbatim, lightly stitched), in connected prose rather than punchy fragments, at the fuller current length. **Pick one option per item, tweak in your own voice, then tell me and I'll build the 3-platform batch JSON** at `analytics/social-media-content-evergreen/next-few-days.json`, condensing each to LinkedIn / Mastodon (<=500) / Bluesky (<=290).

5	Conventions when I build the JSON: the URL goes in the `url` field (no UTM, no inline links; the pipeline adds per-platform UTM), and `image` stays `""` (the pipeline scrapes og:image).
6	
7	**Selection (all `[ ]` in the queue):**
8	- Blog — GenAI Code Quality: Fundamental Flaws and Bluffing (TIER 1)
9	- Blog — The Sprint Backlog: Complete Guide (TIER 2)
10	- Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy (TIER 1)
11	- Glossary — Definition of Done

16	## 1. Blog — GenAI code quality / bluffing
17	**URL:** /blog/genai-code-quality-fundamental-flaws-and-how-bluffing-makes-it-worse/
18	
19	### Option A — the data, and why it's structural
20	AI-generated code has 1.7x more issues, and the GenAI code quality gap is turning into a chasm. That's not a random number, it's from a CodeRabbit research report, which also shows 30-41% more tech debt and 39% more cognitive complexity.
21	
22	These problems are structural. They don't magically fix themselves, when Anthropic releases a new model. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Some teams think TDD is the fix, and others suggest we can code review our way out of this. We can't code review our way out of this mess, because that just puts the burden on humans to tidy up the mess that the AI created.
23	
24	So instead of trying to build quality into code faster, why don't we work on making sure we know what the right product is first? When it comes to the code itself, give the models smaller, more focused tasks, and start with a small set of acceptance criteria for a single feature.
25	
26	What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.
27	
28	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
29	
30	### Option B — the bluffing
31	GenAI code quality problems start with how the models are trained. Training focuses on pass/fail: does the code compile, does it pass the tests? There's no reward for writing code that's easy to maintain. Worse, 0-1 grading schemes incentivize guessing over admitting a lack of knowledge, so the models learn to "bluff" with plausible but overconfident best guesses.
32	
33	OX Security likens this to an army of junior developers, fast and functional, but lacking architectural judgment. So what about TDD? It helps, but it's solving the wrong problem. It forces you to understand the problem before accepting the solution, but it can't tell you whether the feature itself is waste.
34	
35	The next release from Anthropic/OpenAI won't magically solve the problem. The labs aren't prioritizing: well-designed architecture, maintainability, security in context, and respect for your codebase. Until that changes, we deal with what we've got, one small and focused task at a time.
36	
37	What are you doing to survive this mess? I genuinely want to know.
38	
39	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Agile
40	
41	---
42	
43	## 2. Blog — Sprint Backlog
44	**URL:** /blog/the-humble-sprint-backlog/
45	
46	### Option A — ownership
47	Sadly, many Scrum Teams simply use whatever their online Scrum tool feeds them for their Sprint Backlog. This harms the Team's capacity for engagement, because it reinforces the sense that Scrum is happening to them, not something that they choose.
48	
49	Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it, not a tool, and not an outsider. Many teams also benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress. Teams that limit WIP to two or three Product Backlog Items tend to collaborate more, cross-skill faster, and eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint.
50	
51	Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make it even better.
52	
53	#Scrum #ScrumMaster
54	
55	### Option B — anti-patterns
56	Sprint Backlog's are Scrum's most misunderstood artifact. They're not a list of tickets or tasks. (thanks JIRA.) They're intended to be a tool for the team to understand what is going on in their work and how it is progressing. A couple of Sprint Backlog anti-patterns are worth naming, because they're common and they're quiet.
57	
58	When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which item. When all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.
59	
60	The Sprint Backlog also loses its value when it's used for external purposes like reporting. When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work, it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum Team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else. It's a plan by and for the Developers, a real-time picture of the work they plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.
61	
62	Which Sprint Backlog anti-pattern have you seen the most?
63	
64	#Scrum #ProductOwner
65	
66	---
67	
68	## 3. Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy
69	**URL:** /glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/
70	
71	### Option A — the knowledge cliff
72	We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future.
73	
74	When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill, and this affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.
75	
76	NASA has been through this recently. They want to build big rockets again, and they have mountains of documentation, literally 2900 cubic feet, but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it. This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one.
77	
78	So before automating with AI, ask: do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the output? The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.
79	
80	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership
81	
82	### Option B — pilots and radiologists
83	In the academic literature, losing the skills you stop practising is called Deskilling, and we've watched it happen outside software before.
84	
85	In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, they detect problems faster and don't get tired. But too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors who never built the underlying understanding.
86	
87	Pilots have been through this too. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, and automated flight management systems, they reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.
88	
89	Software is walking toward the same cliff, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it. The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.
90	
91	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment
92	
93	---
94	
95	## 4. Glossary — Definition of Done
96	**URL:** /glossary/definition-of-done/
97	
98	### Option A — the pressure
99	The 2020 Scrum Guide elevated Definition of Done to a formal commitment for the Increment. In other words, Done is not optional: it is the team's promise about what "complete" means.
100	
101	The hardest problem to achieving Done is pressure to deliver more features. As the pressure builds, the team may respond by compromising on Done. In the short term this appears to be fine, as they appear to get more work finished. In the long run, the increase in bugs inevitably offsets the value of the added work, and each shortcut accumulates as technical debt, making future work slower and more error-prone.
102	
103	That's why the team need to start Sprint Planning with a clear understanding of their own Definition of Done, and only take on work that they can bring to truly Done.
104	
105	#Scrum #ScrumMaster
106	
107	### Option B — undone work
108	When a product is not truly releasable at the end of Sprint, the difference is often referred to as Undone work. Why is this a problem? It's a problem because it reduces transparency. The Product Owner and clients think the team have completed work on those User Stories, yet the work isn't complete.
109	
110	Here's how that plays out later: a bug is found several Sprints after the code is written, and now new code relies on the defective behaviour. Or, missing a security audit, the application is susceptible to a SQL injection attack. When a team has a rigorous Definition of Done, the Product Owner should be able to release a new version of the product at the end of every Sprint.
111	
112	One caution: Definition of Done is for the Scrum Team to understand the quality of the product they're creating. It's not a reporting standard, and using it as one leads to micro management.
113	
114	#Scrum #ProductOwner
115	
116	---
117	
118	## 5. Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)
119	**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
120	*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Swap in a web-archive link if you'd rather point at the issue itself.)*
121	
122	### Option A — 5% vs 20%
123	By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans. The research suggests that the number should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action.
124	
125	I found that in Chris Bailey's book Intentional, which I read on a hiking trip in the Canary Islands that turned into a reading trip when a storm rolled in. Thinking about Scrum, all of Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are about planning and goal attainment. Officially, they're supposed to occupy 10% of the Sprint, and Backlog Refinement takes up another 3-5%. Scrum anticipated the research that Chris found for his book by more than a decade.
126	
127	When we see teams first adopt Scrum, there is often pushback: too much time spent on planning and not enough time doing. I've always known the pushback was misplaced, and now I have research to support it.
128	
129	#Scrum #Agile
130	
131	### Option B — planning in a GenAI world
132	Many teams are using GenAI to rip through their Product Backlog without considering whether the work has any value. Shipping unproven features faster is not winning.
133	
134	By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans, when the research suggests it should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action. Scrum already builds that in: Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are all about planning and goal attainment, and Backlog Refinement adds a little more.
135	
136	As we move into a world where GenAI can help us do some of the heavy lifting, intentions and planning will be ever more important. To thrive in this new world, we will need better Product Ownership and quality, not just more output.
137	
138	#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner
