Since the Sprint Backlog is solely for the Scrum Team to organize their own work during a Sprint, they are the only ones who create, change, and manage it, not a tool, and not an outsider. Many teams also benefit by stealing a page from the Kanban playbook and limiting Work in Progress. Teams that limit WIP to two or three Product Backlog Items tend to collaborate more, cross-skill faster, and eventually eliminate the problem of having unfinished work at the end of Sprint.

Good Scrum teams know that they own the Sprint Backlog. Great teams experiment every few Sprints to find what they can do to make it even better.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — anti-patterns
Sprint Backlog's are Scrum's most misunderstood artifact. They're not a list of tickets or tasks. (thanks JIRA.) They're intended to be a tool for the team to understand what is going on in their work and how it is progressing. A couple of Sprint Backlog anti-patterns are worth naming, because they're common and they're quiet.

When the Sprint Backlog is created during Sprint Planning, some teams decide who will work on which item. When all items are pre-assigned to team members, we have just planned for the first bottleneck.

The Sprint Backlog also loses its value when it's used for external purposes like reporting. When leadership uses it to look over the shoulders of the people doing the work, it often leads to overloading the Sprint Backlog with details that undermine and eliminate transparency. The Sprint Backlog is used only by the Scrum Team, and is not intended to be viewed by anyone else. It's a plan by and for the Developers, a real-time picture of the work they plan to accomplish to achieve the Sprint Goal.

Which Sprint Backlog anti-pattern have you seen the most?

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 3. Glossary — AI and Skill Atrophy
**URL:** /glossary/ai-skill-atrophy/

### Option A — the knowledge cliff
We're losing skills because we don't use them, and we're not growing the developers of the future.

When you use an LLM to make a decision you could make without the LLM, you gain a sense of false confidence. The easier it is to prompt an LLM to produce an answer, the less we develop the skill, and this affects junior people more than senior people, since they have less overall experience to base their skills on.

NASA has been through this recently. They want to build big rockets again, and they have mountains of documentation, literally 2900 cubic feet, but they don't have the understanding and tacit knowledge to use it. This is a knowledge cliff, and the software industry is headed to one.

So before automating with AI, ask: do we understand the domain well enough to evaluate the output? The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #Leadership

### Option B — pilots and radiologists
In the academic literature, losing the skills you stop practising is called Deskilling, and we've watched it happen outside software before.

In radiology, AI assistants help detect abnormalities in medical images. In theory, they detect problems faster and don't get tired. But too much reliance on AI leaves the radiologist unable to detect on their own. Bad enough for the senior radiologists, but even worse for new doctors who never built the underlying understanding.

Pilots have been through this too. With the advent of autopilot, instrument landing systems, and automated flight management systems, they reduced the need for certain piloting skills. To combat this, they increased the amount of training and simulator time for pilots to maintain their certifications.

Software is walking toward the same cliff, except we're cutting practice instead of protecting it. The more we use AI, the more critical thinking becomes important.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment

---

## 4. Glossary — Definition of Done
**URL:** /glossary/definition-of-done/

### Option A — the pressure
The 2020 Scrum Guide elevated Definition of Done to a formal commitment for the Increment. In other words, Done is not optional: it is the team's promise about what "complete" means.

The hardest problem to achieving Done is pressure to deliver more features. As the pressure builds, the team may respond by compromising on Done. In the short term this appears to be fine, as they appear to get more work finished. In the long run, the increase in bugs inevitably offsets the value of the added work, and each shortcut accumulates as technical debt, making future work slower and more error-prone.

That's why the team need to start Sprint Planning with a clear understanding of their own Definition of Done, and only take on work that they can bring to truly Done.

#Scrum #ScrumMaster

### Option B — undone work
When a product is not truly releasable at the end of Sprint, the difference is often referred to as Undone work. Why is this a problem? It's a problem because it reduces transparency. The Product Owner and clients think the team have completed work on those User Stories, yet the work isn't complete.

Here's how that plays out later: a bug is found several Sprints after the code is written, and now new code relies on the defective behaviour. Or, missing a security audit, the application is susceptible to a SQL injection attack. When a team has a rigorous Definition of Done, the Product Owner should be able to release a new version of the product at the end of every Sprint.

One caution: Definition of Done is for the Scrum Team to understand the quality of the product they're creating. It's not a reporting standard, and using it as one leads to micro management.

#Scrum #ProductOwner

---

## 5. Newsletter — "Are You Planning Enough?" (2026-04-02)
**URL:** /newsletter-subscribe/
*(Newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so this drives to signup. Swap in a web-archive link if you'd rather point at the issue itself.)*

### Option A — 5% vs 20%
By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans. The research suggests that the number should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action.

I found that in Chris Bailey's book Intentional, which I read on a hiking trip in the Canary Islands that turned into a reading trip when a storm rolled in. Thinking about Scrum, all of Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are about planning and goal attainment. Officially, they're supposed to occupy 10% of the Sprint, and Backlog Refinement takes up another 3-5%. Scrum anticipated the research that Chris found for his book by more than a decade.

When we see teams first adopt Scrum, there is often pushback: too much time spent on planning and not enough time doing. I've always known the pushback was misplaced, and now I have research to support it.

#Scrum #Agile

### Option B — planning in a GenAI world
Many teams are using GenAI to rip through their Product Backlog without considering whether the work has any value. Shipping unproven features faster is not winning.

By default, as humans we spend about 5% of our time planning and 95% implementing those plans, when the research suggests it should be closer to 20% planning and 80% action. Scrum already builds that in: Sprint Planning, Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum are all about planning and goal attainment, and Backlog Refinement adds a little more.

As we move into a world where GenAI can help us do some of the heavy lifting, intentions and planning will be ever more important. To thrive in this new world, we will need better Product Ownership and quality, not just more output.

#AIinSoftwareDevelopment #ProductOwner

---
title: "Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity"
date: "2026-07-10"

---
import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import Loopy from '@/components/global/Loopy.astro';
import genAIGambling from '@/content/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/images/GenAIGamblingWithYourProductivity.png';

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. “Increase Canada’s business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports.”[^2] I’m reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. A target like this invites AI washing: measure success by adoption rate and organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create “outsized value”: healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

<Figure
  src={genAIGambling}
  alt="Illustration of a robot labelled AI next to a pair of dice, headed “Canada's AI Strategy: Will AI Make Us More Productive?” and captioned “Gambling with Your Productivity”"
  caption="Naming sectors without evidence of where AI actually helps is a bet, not a plan."
/>

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it’s the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn’t make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we’ve sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn’t make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation.

Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go: walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

These factors don’t sit in neat boxes; they feed each other. Drag any node in the diagram below to see how a change ripples through the system. Notice the reinforcing loop on the left: admin burden burns doctors out, so fewer family doctors remain, which piles more admin on those still practising. That shortage pushes people into the ER, and the beds, our real bottleneck, stay full whether or not triage runs faster.

<Loopy
  data="[[[1,440,270,0.5,%22Family%2520Doctors%22,3],[2,200,410,0.5,%22Admin%2520Burden%22,1],[3,200,150,0.5,%22Doctor%2520Burnout%22,0],[4,660,150,0.5,%22ER%2520Visits%22,2],[5,880,300,0.5,%22Bed%2520Occupancy%22,0],[6,660,430,0.5,%22LTC%2520Waitlist%22,5]],[[2,3,40,1],[3,1,40,-1],[1,2,150,-1],[1,4,-40,-1],[4,5,-40,1],[6,5,40,1]],[[200,500,%22Reinforcing%2520loop%22],[880,190,%22The%2520bottleneck%22]],7%5D"
  title="Causal loop diagram: why faster ER triage doesn't empty full hospital beds"
/>

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system.

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they’re paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here’s the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it “AI” but it’s not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.

AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity.

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don’t cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) In an attempt to reduce the unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of [GenAI making us feel more productive](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/) without making a big difference.

GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can’t keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can’t expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds.

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)

Inbox zero was sold to us by productivity experts, and yet it never seems to happen in real life. When we take a step back, the pattern becomes clear: Fast responses to email -> People learn you get stuff done -> More requests for your help appear in your inbox -> ... . Without a fancy label, we engaged in Systems Thinking, a mental model that looks at a problem not in isolation but as a series of interconnected parts. For once, I will find a use for GenAI. (Using GenAI as a sparring partner for Systems Thinking is a core practice in our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/).)
<Figure
  src={CLDForInboxOverwhelm}
  alt="Systems Thinking Causal Loop Diagram showing email inbox overwhelm feedback loop"
  caption="Systems Thinking Causal Loop Diagram showing email inbox overwhelm feedback loop"
  align='right'
/>

## What is Systems Thinking in the Agile World?
Systems Thinking is a mental model that views problems as interconnected parts
rather than isolated issues, it means:
- Looking beyond surface symptoms to find deeper causes
- Understanding how changes in one area affect others
- Identifying feedback loops that create recurring problems
- Avoiding local optimization at the expense of the overall system

## Systems Thinking in Scrum Master Training
In [CSM workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), my final major exercise is to give attendees a coaching problem and ask them to consider how they would coach through it.

Throughout the workshop, we cover team-level improvements through:
- Retrospectives and clear action items
- Working Agreements to clarify how we work together
- Improving Product Backlog Refinement
- Sprint Backlogs and improving flow
- Definition of Done and improving quality
- Most groups even ask questions that get us to discuss what motivates people
- ... the list goes on

Most of these are clear and likely sources of improvement for a good Scrum Master. The final exercise is intended to take them to a higher level, helping them start thinking about the bigger picture and ask why some challenges are recurring problems. The group is given one of several stories about teams that are struggling, and they're invited to help coach the fictional team. The problems are challenging enough that small improvements at the team level are helpful, but not enough. The idea is to consider many real problems at work and to understand the bigger picture.

My goal is to introduce the attendees to the rudiments of Systems thinking. I give people just a few questions:
- What happened weeks ago? months ago? years ago? Many challenges are buried years in the past.
- If this continues, what will the effects be in months? years? Delay effects are especially interesting as they hide cause and effect.
- Use different perspectives? How would someone with a different background see this situation? How would a manager see it? A senior executive?
- If we looked from 30,000 ft, what would it look like?
- What assumptions are we making?
- ...

There isn't a complete list of questions; I normally suggest attendees look at the Water's Centre System Thinking Cards[^1]. However, it's hard to keep the questions in mind while exploring a problem. I've been using systems thinking as a lens or mental model for years, and I still forget to ask some of the questions. For someone new, the whole thing can be intimidating, and that isn't good.

## Using GenAI as a Systems Thinking Coach
I've been thinking about how GenAI can aid critical thinking rather than generate more slop. That is when I realized I could create a set of prompts to help with using Systems Thinking as a mental model. I created it as a Claude Skill[^2], so that it can be added to your Claude environment and always be available for use. (The standard has been adopted by OpenAI and others, as [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/home) so without too much effort, you should be able to use the skill in most LLMs)

Since most people in a workshop don't already have Claude Code running, they just copied my Claude skill text: https://github.com/mlevison/systems-thinking -- specifically this file: references/questions-of-a-systems-thinker.md and put it at the start of their conversations

I also crafted a challenging situation where I thought Systems thinking would help. Let's run with an example here:

<HighlightBox heading="Our Fictional Problem" variant="caseStudy">
## Case Study: Horizontally Stratified Teams
A senior architect is trapped in what he calls a "vicious death spiral." His project connects to dozens of external systems, and the Scrum Master decided to split the work: one team handles user stories while another manages technical integrations. Six sprints in, refinement and planning sessions routinely exceed eight hours. Stories arrive incomplete, missing critical integration details. The technical team launches into deep dives the story team can't follow. Meanwhile, the story team keeps surfacing requirements that expose unexpected integration challenges. Dependencies bounce between groups, estimates become guesswork, and team members mentally check out around hour five.

The architect has watched the same story carry over three sprints because the slicing never works. The Scrum Master keeps extending sessions, believing more time will surface all hidden complexity. The architect is convinced there must be a way to groom, slice, and size stories in under ten minutes. He just can't see how to get there from here.
</HighlightBox>
As usual with a GenAI model, the conversation is long. I'm excerpting key details and then sharing my response.
> Let me start with a foundational question: What organizational forces or constraints led to the decision to horizontally stratify teams in the first place?

**My response:** In the past, before Scrum, the whole stratified by specialized teams. Since Scrum has come in, nothing has changed. Everyone says it is just more efficient.
> The phrase "everyone says it is just more efficient" is particularly telling—it points to an unexamined mental model that may be creating a self-reinforcing loop.
> ...
> Question for you: When people say "it's more efficient," what evidence are they using? Are they measuring:
> - Individual utilization rates? (people staying busy in their specialty)
> - Or actual throughput of completed, valuable features to customers?

**My response:** They're measuring how much work (output) each person gets done.
> There it is. This is a classic systems thinking trap called local optimization at the expense of global optimization. The organization is measuring output (how busy each specialist is) but not outcome (how quickly customer value flows through the system).
>...
> What's happening to the people in this system? You mentioned team members "checking out mentally around hour five." What are you observing in terms of morale, turnover, or people's sense of effectiveness?

**My response:** At the start of each big release people are enthusiastic. As release wears on, priorities change and the pressure to get everything done increases.

<CalloutBox heading="The following was the most insightful element of the whole exchange">
>The system keeps trying to solve a structure problem with a process problem.
>
>**Question for you**:
> When a release ends—does the organization do retrospectives or post-mortems? And if so, what explanations do people give for why things took longer than expected?
> Do they say:
> - "Requirements weren't clear enough"
> - "We didn't plan well enough"
>- "The technology was more complex than we thought"
>
> Or do they ever say:
>  - "Our team structure creates coordination overhead we're not accounting for"?
</CalloutBox>
**My response:** They tend to comment on the requirements because that is another department.

## Visualizing Problems with Causal Loop Diagrams
This could go on forever, and the [conversation was already over 300 lines](/sample-systems-thinking-conversation/), so I asked: "Before we go any further, let's visualize what we have so far with a Causal Loop diagram". Diagrams in the Markdown world are typically done with Mermaid (what a name), and so I rendered them with the free Mermaid editor
<Figure
  src={CLDForHorizontalTeam}
  alt="Causal Loop Diagram showing local optimization trap in horizontally stratified Scrum teams"
  caption="Causal Loop Diagram showing local optimization trap in horizontally stratified Scrum teams"
  align='right'
/>

This picture illustrates some of the key challenges in the conversation and would make a good starting point for further conversation.
## Conclusion: Using GenAI for Deeper Team Analysis
Be careful of taking the outputs of the model too seriously, remember its only job is to predict the next most likely token, it has no understanding. In addition, if you read the [much longer version of the conversation](/sample-systems-thinking-conversation/), you will see the model made a few logical leaps that would need to be checked.

## Systems Thinking a Claude Skill
The skill is found in the repo: [Systems Thinking Skill for Claude Code](https://github.com/mlevison/systems-thinking). Please Github issues to make suggestions.

## Conclusion: Using GenAI for Deeper Team Analysis
Systems Thinking is most helpful when it is part of a conversation among a group working on a problem together. It is a tool that helps build a shared understanding of the world. The intention of this skill is to make it easier to have those conversations and to ask questions that might have been missed. Please use this with others and not in isolation.

[^1]: Waters Centre Systems Thinking Cards: https://thinkingtoolsstudio.waterscenterst.org/cards
[^2]: Claude Skills are specialized instruction sets that teach Claude how to excel at specific tasks - like creating professional documents, building presentations, or analyzing systems. A big benefit is that skills are only loaded into Claude's working memory when needed. So our Systems Thinking skill sits in the background, and Claude will pull it in when your conversation calls for it. This saves on tokens and makes it's use more efficient.

_Scrum team **Working Agreements** are a simple, powerful way of creating explicit guidelines for what kind of work culture you want for your Team. They are a reminder for everyone about how they can commit to respectful behaviour and communication. In this post we'll see how the fictional World's Smallest Online Bookstore (WSOBS) Scrum team struggles without a Working Agreement, and why having one would be useful._

Acceptance Criteria

<HighlightBox heading="Dramatis Personae" variant="caseStudy">
**Steve:** - A scrumMaster and the hero of our story

**Paula:** - The Product Owner of Steve's team

**Kirby** – one of the Team's software developers

**Tonia** – the Team's Quality Assurance specialist

**Doug** – another of the Team's software developers

**Ian** – the Team's Business Logic programming specialist
</HighlightBox>

In the past few Sprints, there have been moments of social friction noticed by both Steve and the rest of the WSOBS Team. They included:

Kirby was blunt when discussing a defect with both Tonia and Ian.

Some discussions with the whole Team became so heated that the quieter team members stopped speaking up for several days.

Doug was late for Daily Scrum on several days.

On multiple occasions, Team members needed to ask Paula some questions, but she wasn't available by email, and they often didn't know how to find her.

None of these individual issues was truly bad, however, taken together and left unchecked, they harm the Team's cohesion. When that happens, people opt to stay silent when there is an opportunity to share an opinion, and events like Daily Scrum becomes less useful when Team members signal their disrespect by frequently being late.

During the next Retrospective, Steve mentions a few of these issues and says that he wants to talk about making their environment better. Tonia shares that she knows another one of their peer teams has created their own Working Agreement to reduce some of the friction and improve respect.

Before we see how Steve helps his team in this episode, let's make sure we understand what a Working Agreement is, and should be.

## What is a Working Agreement?

A Working Agreement is a short set of guidelines created by the Scrum Team, that establishes what the expectations of the team members are for one another. A well-written Agreement should help establish and reinforce a clear, shared understanding about what team members agree is good behaviour and communication.

## Why do Working Agreements Matter?

Working Agreements help make implicit social expectations explicit. (Whoa, that's a mouthful.) They invite team members to tell each other what matters to them on a whole host of topics. This leads to a shared understanding and, in return, a reduction in friction. Done well, they also invite open and honest communication which helps create psychological safety.

## Characteristics of an Effective Scrum Team Working Agreement

A Working Agreement doesn't have a police force to ensure that it's followed. Its effectiveness comes from being:

- **Public and Visible** – preferably written in a large font and posted in a prominent space (perhaps where Daily Stand-up takes place)
- **Collaborative** – created by all, not imposed by others
- **Short** – a small list of agreements that are easily remembered and lived up to trumps a big list that overwhelms people and gets forgotten
- **Updated Frequently** – [Taiichi Ohno](https://blog.gembaacademy.com/2010/02/16/excerpts_from_an_interview_with_taiichi_ohno_july_1/) once said: "If the kanbans do not change for one month, you are salary thieves"
- **Consequential** – when the agreements are violated, Team members call out the violation with respectful reminders

## Working Agreements Should be Unique to Team Needs
Each Scrum Team will create its own Working Agreement based on the context of its work. Elements of an Agreement might include some of these examples:

- **Core hours** – times during the day that all Team members agree to be present and available for collaboration.
- **Daily Standup** – the time that it happens.
- **Attendance** for meetings or events – whether or not you agree to support decisions made. in your absence, whether you will let your team know in advance if you can't attend.
- **Product Owner** – availability and contact information.
- **Definition of Done** - an agreement about quality
- How the Team **limits Work in Progress**.
- How the Team ensures everyone has an **equal voice** and feels respected. For example, use of a talking stick, where the person who has the stick has the opportunity to talk and everyone else focuses on them. My favorite tool is a bean bag or ball that can easily be tossed from person to person, rather than a stick.
- **Decision-Making** Process and Rules - establish a clear process for making decisions: consensus-based decision-making or voting mechanisms as needed. (See [Why Group Decision-Making Techniques are Important](/blog/why-are-group-decision-making-techniques-important/) for more depth.)
- **Skill development** – maybe it's agreed that during each Sprint at least one Team Member will work on growing a skill outside of their core strengths.
- **Technical Debt** - in the case of software development, maybe there's an element that states every Sprint the Team will make an effort to improve some part of their codebase.
- **Impediments** - Guidelines for handling them.
- An understanding of how to resolve **conflict** – for example, ask for a facilitator, or echo back your understanding of the other person's viewpoint, etc.
- **Handling Outside Interruptions** - define procedures for managing interruptions during the Sprint itself, such as setting expectations with stakeholders and limiting distractions within the team.
- **Sustainable Pace** - how can the team ensure that they're committing to work that is realistically achievable in the Sprint?
- **Team Values** - review the Scrum Values and decide how they apply in your world. As a reminder, the Scrum Values are "Focus, Commitment, Courage, Openness and Respect". Many teams also discuss topics that include collaboration, continuous learning, and customer focus.
- **Communication Channels** - agree on preferred communication channels (e.g. Slack, Microsoft Teams) for day-to-day interactions and set expectations around response times. (_Hint: instant response is unhealthy._)
- **Collaboration Tools** - choose appropriate tools (e.g. Mural, Miro) to facilitate team collaboration and ensure everyone has access to them.

13	Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]
14	
15	The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. “Increase Canada’s business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports.”[^2] I’m reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. A target like this invites AI washing: measure success by adoption rate and organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.

19	## Sectors
20	The strategy names sectors where AI will create “outsized value”: healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

28	There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

Assuming the AI doesn’t make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we’ve sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn’t make a meaningful difference.
32	
33	Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation.

35	Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
36	- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
37	- Why are hospital beds so full?

41	- Waiting lists for long term care
42	- Staffing shortages

60	- Emergency Department volume
61	- Bed allocations and assignments
62	- Room cleaning
63	- Critical care capacity
64	- Surgical scheduling
65	- Discharge planning
66	
67	Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.
68	
69	GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.
70	
71	AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here’s the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it “AI” but it’s not the AI the strategy is betting on.
72	
73	The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.
74	
75	AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.
76	
77	### Family Doctors and GenAI
78	Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity.
79	
80	After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.
81	
82	Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don’t cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) In an attempt to reduce the unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of [GenAI making us feel more productive](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/) without making a big difference.
83	
84	GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.
85	
86	Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.
87	
88	We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.
89	
90	## Not a Magic Wand
91	GenAI isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).
92	
93	Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can’t keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can’t expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds.
94	
95	The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.
96

98	[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)

---
title: "Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity"
date: "2026-07-10"
categories:
  - "artificial-intelligence"
coverImage: '@/content/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/images/GenAIGamblingWithYourProductivity.png'
excerpt: There is a massive gap between claiming AI will boost productivity and actually fixing bottlenecks. Lessons from Canada's healthcare system and Humber River Hospital.
---
import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import Loopy from '@/components/global/Loopy.astro';
import genAIGambling from '@/content/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/images/GenAIGamblingWithYourProductivity.png';

Canada has a real productivity problem. We have for decades. In 1984, the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked. In 2022, it had fallen to 71%.[^1]

The new AI strategy is an attempt to fix that. It promises a 3 percent increase in GDP, from labour productivity. “Increase Canada’s business adoption of AI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034, through boosting SMEs and business adoption supports.”[^2] I’m reminded of the mineshaft gap in Dr Strangelove (Stanley Kubrick was satirizing the military focus on the missile gap in the 1950s). Adoption of AI doesn’t make an organization more productive. I made [the same argument about the federal government](/blog/will-ai-make-the-federal-government-more-efficient-or-just-more-busy/): dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess. A target like this invites AI washing: measure success by adoption rate and organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn’t make it so.

## Sectors
The strategy names sectors where AI will create “outsized value”: healthcare, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing. Why these sectors? Based on what evidence?

<Figure
  src={genAIGambling}
  alt="Illustration of a robot labelled AI next to a pair of dice, headed “Canada's AI Strategy: Will AI Make Us More Productive?” and captioned “Gambling with Your Productivity”"
  caption="Naming sectors without evidence of where AI actually helps is a bet, not a plan."
/>

There are many ways AI could help and harm in all of these sectors. The strategy doesn’t say anything useful about how AI will help.

## Healthcare
I will focus on the health sector, because it’s the one we hear about most often. In Ontario, the stories are of emergency rooms overflowing. In some rural communities, the emergency rooms operate on reduced hours due to staffing shortages. To make the emergency room more efficient, we might try to use AI to help in the triage process. Assuming the AI doesn’t make any mistakes (unwise assumption), we’ve sped up the triage process. Unfortunately if the hospital is operating at 100% or more of capacity in terms of the number of beds, speeding triage doesn’t help. It helps a handful leave faster but doesn’t make a meaningful difference.

Our mistake? We tackled the emergency room problem in isolation.

Putting on our [Systems Thinking](/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) hat, we want to ask two questions:
- Why are there so many people visiting emergency rooms?
- Why are hospital beds so full?

### Hospital beds
- Low population to hospital bed ratio
- Waiting lists for long term care
- Staffing shortages

### Emergency Room Volume
- Lack of family doctor
- Lack of family doctor turns simple problems into more complex problems, which in turn might result in a hospital stay
- Unsure where to go: walk in clinic? Emergency?
- Seasonal flu et al

These factors don’t sit in neat boxes; they feed each other. Drag any node in the diagram below to see how a change ripples through the system. Notice the reinforcing loop on the left: admin burden burns doctors out, so fewer family doctors remain, which piles more admin on those still practising. That shortage pushes people into the ER, and the beds, our real bottleneck, stay full whether or not triage runs faster.

<Loopy
  data="[[[1,440,270,0.5,%22Family%2520Doctors%22,3],[2,200,410,0.5,%22Admin%2520Burden%22,1],[3,200,150,0.5,%22Doctor%2520Burnout%22,0],[4,660,150,0.5,%22ER%2520Visits%22,2],[5,880,300,0.5,%22Bed%2520Occupancy%22,0],[6,660,430,0.5,%22LTC%2520Waitlist%22,5]],[[2,3,40,1],[3,1,40,-1],[1,2,150,-1],[1,4,-40,-1],[4,5,-40,1],[6,5,40,1]],[[200,500,%22Reinforcing%2520loop%22],[880,190,%22The%2520bottleneck%22]],7%5D"
  title="Causal loop diagram: why faster ER triage doesn't empty full hospital beds"
/>

None of these problems will magically get fixed by AI. If we want our healthcare system to help us get well/stay well, look at the overall system.

One example of a hospital taking a systemic approach? Humber River Hospital has a command centre where they’re paying attention[^3] to:
- Emergency Department volume
- Bed allocations and assignments
- Room cleaning
- Critical care capacity
- Surgical scheduling
- Discharge planning

Reading the promotional PDF from GE[^4] the command centre is focused on getting the patients who need admission a bed faster and reducing pain, complications and secondary infections.

GE promotes this system as using AI. However, the AI isn’t the central feature. The value of this system is that people in the hospital are paying constant attention to how the hospital is working. If there is a constraint, they make changes to reduce the problem. The command centre is staffed by a cross disciplinary group of people, so that there is enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions.

AI is useful here, because they’ve studied the flow of the system. They’ve established useful metrics: getting people healthy and allowing them to leave hospital. Here’s the irony: the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT and GenAI entirely. GE brands it “AI” but it’s not the AI the strategy is betting on.

The material available in public is promotional so the actual effectiveness of the real system is something I can’t see.

AI didn’t make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

### Family Doctors and GenAI
Earlier we noted that the lack of family doctors is a contributing factor to over capacity.

After a full day of seeing patients, family doctors still have to write up charts documenting their findings, treatment and prescriptions. This is unpaid labour, the doctor is paid for the patient visit and the documentation is treated as overhead.

Family doctors are already dealing with burnout, it turns out that OHIP payments in many cases don’t cover the realistic costs of running a clinic (rental, front office staff, medical equipment, computers, etc.) In an attempt to reduce the unpaid labour, many doctors I know have turned to GenAI transcription tools. There are clearly documented problems with some of these tools making mistakes with both the diagnoses and medications[^5]. Yet the physicians I know report saving a considerable amount of time. Possibly another example of [GenAI making us feel more productive](/blog/using-genai-to-code-not-so-fast/) without making a big difference.

GenAI might help here, however we’ve solved a symptom. Family doctors are expected to run businesses (not their training) and are expected to handle a large number of administrative tasks along with seeing patients.

Transcription tools may help, but they don’t solve the underlying problem. The administrative burden on family doctors is a major factor in their burnout.

We need to fix the system, and not just the symptoms.

## Not a Magic Wand
GenAI isn’t a magic wand and it isn’t a panacea. In the right context, it can be very useful. Used in the wrong place, it can [make an organization more fragile, not more resilient](/blog/is-ai-making-your-organization-fragile-or-more-resilient/).

Humber River Hospital’s command centre is a good step in the right direction. If we want to make a meaningful difference in the healthcare system, we need to look wider than just an emergency room. In short, we want to understand why family doctors are leaving the profession. If we can’t keep them happy to stay in the profession, then we can’t expect to keep patients out of the emergency room. At the other end of the spectrum, since many hospital beds are occupied by patients waiting for long term care, we need to find compassionate ways to improve the long term care system. We may also need more hospital staff and more beds.

The Healthcare system in Canada is just one example of many. We have a productivity problem, but we can’t just tell people to use GenAI and expect an improvement. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks in the system and focus on eliminating that bottleneck.

[^1]: Bank of Canada, [Time to Break the Glass: Fixing Canada's Productivity Problem](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2024/03/time-to-break-the-glass-fixing-canadas-productivity-problem/)
[^2]: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, [Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all)
[^3]: Humber River Hospital Foundation, [Humber River Hospital's Command Centre Has Created 23 Virtual Beds](https://www.hrhfoundation.ca/blog/humber-river-hospitals-command-centre-has-created-23-virtual-beds/)
[^4]: GE Healthcare, [Humber River Hospital Command Centre: One Year in Review](https://www.gehealthcare.com/content/dam/gehc/sitecore-migrated-assets/gehc/us/files/services/value-partnerships/20190121-humber-river-hospital-command-centre-one-year-in-review.pdf) (PDF)
[^5]: CBC News, [Medical AI transcriber for Ontario doctors 'hallucinated,' generated errors: auditor general](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/ai-scribe-system-hallucinations-9.7197049)

1	---
2	title: "Systems Thinking with GenAI: Solve Deep Team Problems"
3	date: "2026-01-22"
4	lastUpdated: '2026-01-22'
5	categories:
6	- "artificial-intelligence"
7	coverImage: "@/content/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/images/causal-loop-diagram-for-inbox.png"
8	excerpt: 'GenAI helps you apply Systems Thinking to team problems. Understand the interconnected parts and avoid common traps like local optimization.'
9	---
10	
11	import CalloutBox from '@/components/global/callout-box.astro';
12	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
13	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
14	import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
15	import CLDForInboxOverwhelm from '@/content/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/images/causal-loop-diagram-for-inbox.png'
16	import CLDForHorizontalTeam from '@/content/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/images/causal-loop-diagram-for-horizontal-team.png'
17	
18	Inbox zero was sold to us by productivity experts, and yet it never seems to happen in real life. When we take a step back, the pattern becomes clear: Fast responses to email -> People learn you get stuff done -> More requests for your help appear in your inbox -> ... . Without a fancy label, we engaged in Systems Thinking, a mental model that looks at a problem not in isolation but as a series of interconnected parts. For once, I will find a use for GenAI. (Using GenAI as a sparring partner for Systems Thinking is a core practice in our [Surviving the AI Tsunami course](/surviving-the-ai-tsunami-an-evidenced-based-course/).)
19	<Figure
20	  src={CLDForInboxOverwhelm}
21	  alt="Systems Thinking Causal Loop Diagram showing email inbox overwhelm feedback loop"
22	  caption="Systems Thinking Causal Loop Diagram showing email inbox overwhelm feedback loop"
23	  align='right'
24	/>
25	
26	## What is Systems Thinking in the Agile World?
27	Systems Thinking is a mental model that views problems as interconnected parts
28	rather than isolated issues, it means:
29	- Looking beyond surface symptoms to find deeper causes
30	- Understanding how changes in one area affect others
31	- Identifying feedback loops that create recurring problems
32	- Avoiding local optimization at the expense of the overall system
33	
34	## Systems Thinking in Scrum Master Training
35	In [CSM workshops](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/), my final major exercise is to give attendees a coaching problem and ask them to consider how they would coach through it.
36	
37	Throughout the workshop, we cover team-level improvements through:
38	- Retrospectives and clear action items
39	- Working Agreements to clarify how we work together
40	- Improving Product Backlog Refinement
41	- Sprint Backlogs and improving flow
42	- Definition of Done and improving quality
43	- Most groups even ask questions that get us to discuss what motivates people
44	- ... the list goes on
45	
46	Most of these are clear and likely sources of improvement for a good Scrum Master. The final exercise is intended to take them to a higher level, helping them start thinking about the bigger picture and ask why some challenges are recurring problems. The group is given one of several stories about teams that are struggling, and they're invited to help coach the fictional team. The problems are challenging enough that small improvements at the team level are helpful, but not enough. The idea is to consider many real problems at work and to understand the bigger picture.
47	
48	My goal is to introduce the attendees to the rudiments of Systems thinking. I give people just a few questions:
49	- What happened weeks ago? months ago? years ago? Many challenges are buried years in the past.
50	- If this continues, what will the effects be in months? years? Delay effects are especially interesting as they hide cause and effect.
51	- Use different perspectives? How would someone with a different background see this situation? How would a manager see it? A senior executive?
52	- If we looked from 30,000 ft, what would it look like?
53	- What assumptions are we making?
54	- ...
55	
56	There isn't a complete list of questions; I normally suggest attendees look at the Water's Centre System Thinking Cards[^1]. However, it's hard to keep the questions in mind while exploring a problem. I've been using systems thinking as a lens or mental model for years, and I still forget to ask some of the questions. For someone new, the whole thing can be intimidating, and that isn't good.
57	
58	## Using GenAI as a Systems Thinking Coach
59	I've been thinking about how GenAI can aid critical thinking rather than generate more slop. That is when I realized I could create a set of prompts to help with using Systems Thinking as a mental model. I created it as a Claude Skill[^2], so that it can be added to your Claude environment and always be available for use. (The standard has been adopted by OpenAI and others, as [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/home) so without too much effort, you should be able to use the skill in most LLMs)
60	
61	Since most people in a workshop don't already have Claude Code running, they just copied my Claude skill text: https://github.com/mlevison/systems-thinking -- specifically this file: references/questions-of-a-systems-thinker.md and put it at the start of their conversations
62	
63	I also crafted a challenging situation where I thought Systems thinking would help. Let's run with an example here:
64	
65	<HighlightBox heading="Our Fictional Problem" variant="caseStudy">
66	## Case Study: Horizontally Stratified Teams
67	A senior architect is trapped in what he calls a "vicious death spiral." His project connects to dozens of external systems, and the Scrum Master decided to split the work: one team handles user stories while another manages technical integrations. Six sprints in, refinement and planning sessions routinely exceed eight hours. Stories arrive incomplete, missing critical integration details. The technical team launches into deep dives the story team can't follow. Meanwhile, the story team keeps surfacing requirements that expose unexpected integration challenges. Dependencies bounce between groups, estimates become guesswork, and team members mentally check out around hour five.
68	
69	The architect has watched the same story carry over three sprints because the slicing never works. The Scrum Master keeps extending sessions, believing more time will surface all hidden complexity. The architect is convinced there must be a way to groom, slice, and size stories in under ten minutes. He just can't see how to get there from here.
70	</HighlightBox>
71	As usual with a GenAI model, the conversation is long. I'm excerpting key details and then sharing my response.
72	> Let me start with a foundational question: What organizational forces or constraints led to the decision to horizontally stratify teams in the first place?
73	
74	**My response:** In the past, before Scrum, the whole stratified by specialized teams. Since Scrum has come in, nothing has changed. Everyone says it is just more efficient.
75	> The phrase "everyone says it is just more efficient" is particularly telling—it points to an unexamined mental model that may be creating a self-reinforcing loop.
76	> ...
77	> Question for you: When people say "it's more efficient," what evidence are they using? Are they measuring:
78	> - Individual utilization rates? (people staying busy in their specialty)
79	> - Or actual throughput of completed, valuable features to customers?
80	
81	**My response:** They're measuring how much work (output) each person gets done.
82	> There it is. This is a classic systems thinking trap called local optimization at the expense of global optimization. The organization is measuring output (how busy each specialist is) but not outcome (how quickly customer value flows through the system).
83	>...
84	> What's happening to the people in this system? You mentioned team members "checking out mentally around hour five." What are you observing in terms of morale, turnover, or people's sense of effectiveness?
85	
86	**My response:** At the start of each big release people are enthusiastic. As release wears on, priorities change and the pressure to get everything done increases.
87	
88	<CalloutBox heading="The following was the most insightful element of the whole exchange">
89	>The system keeps trying to solve a structure problem with a process problem.
90	>
91	>**Question for you**:
92	> When a release ends—does the organization do retrospectives or post-mortems? And if so, what explanations do people give for why things took longer than expected?
93	> Do they say:
94	> - "Requirements weren't clear enough"
95	> - "We didn't plan well enough"
96	>- "The technology was more complex than we thought"
97	>
98	> Or do they ever say:
99	>  - "Our team structure creates coordination overhead we're not accounting for"?
100	</CalloutBox>
101	**My response:** They tend to comment on the requirements because that is another department.
102	
103	## Visualizing Problems with Causal Loop Diagrams
104	This could go on forever, and the [conversation was already over 300 lines](/sample-systems-thinking-conversation/), so I asked: "Before we go any further, let's visualize what we have so far with a Causal Loop diagram". Diagrams in the Markdown world are typically done with Mermaid (what a name), and so I rendered them with the free Mermaid editor
105	<Figure
106	  src={CLDForHorizontalTeam}
107	  alt="Causal Loop Diagram showing local optimization trap in horizontally stratified Scrum teams"
108	  caption="Causal Loop Diagram showing local optimization trap in horizontally stratified Scrum teams"
109	  align='right'
110	/>
111	
112	This picture illustrates some of the key challenges in the conversation and would make a good starting point for further conversation.
113	## Conclusion: Using GenAI for Deeper Team Analysis
114	Be careful of taking the outputs of the model too seriously, remember its only job is to predict the next most likely token, it has no understanding. In addition, if you read the [much longer version of the conversation](/sample-systems-thinking-conversation/), you will see the model made a few logical leaps that would need to be checked.
115	
116	## Systems Thinking a Claude Skill
117	The skill is found in the repo: [Systems Thinking Skill for Claude Code](https://github.com/mlevison/systems-thinking). Please Github issues to make suggestions.
118	
119	## Conclusion: Using GenAI for Deeper Team Analysis
120	Systems Thinking is most helpful when it is part of a conversation among a group working on a problem together. It is a tool that helps build a shared understanding of the world. The intention of this skill is to make it easier to have those conversations and to ask questions that might have been missed. Please use this with others and not in isolation.
121	
122	[^1]: Waters Centre Systems Thinking Cards: https://thinkingtoolsstudio.waterscenterst.org/cards
123	[^2]: Claude Skills are specialized instruction sets that teach Claude how to excel at specific tasks - like creating professional documents, building presentations, or analyzing systems. A big benefit is that skills are only loaded into Claude's working memory when needed. So our Systems Thinking skill sits in the background, and Claude will pull it in when your conversation calls for it. This saves on tokens and makes it's use more efficient.
124	
125	<LinkList heading = "Related Blog Entries">
126	    - Systems Thinking is much more useful than [AI Chatbots for Agile Coaches: Why They Fail](/blog/ai-chatbots-for-agile-coaches-why-they-fail/)
127	    - [GenAI and the Feature Factory: Automating Away Collaboration](/blog/gen-ai-and-the-feature-factory-automating-away-collaboration/) - a systems problem where local optimization harms the whole
128	    - [Agile Bonuses - The Damage They Do](/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/) - is an example of Systems Thinking
129	    - [Scrum Anti-Patterns: Micromanagement](/blog/scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement/)
130	    - [Hidden Complexity Tax: How It Kills Organizational Resilience](/blog/how-hidden-complexity-tax-saps-organization-resilience/)
131	    - [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/) - Systems Thinking applied to healthcare bottlenecks
132	</LinkList>
133

My goal is to introduce the attendees to the rudiments of Systems thinking. I give people just a few questions:
- What happened weeks ago? months ago? years ago? Many challenges are buried years in the past.
- If this continues, what will the effects be in months? years? Delay effects are especially interesting as they hide cause and effect.
- Use different perspectives? How would someone with a different background see this situation? How would a manager see it? A senior executive?
- If we looked from 30,000 ft, what would it look like?
- What assumptions are we making?
- ...

There isn't a complete list of questions; I normally suggest attendees look at the Water's Centre System Thinking Cards[^1]. However, it's hard to keep the questions in mind while exploring a problem. I've been using systems thinking as a lens or mental model for years, and I still forget to ask some of the questions. For someone new, the whole thing can be intimidating, and that isn't good.

## Using GenAI as a Systems Thinking Coach
I've been thinking about how GenAI can aid critical thinking rather than generate more slop. That is when I realized I could create a set of prompts to help with using Systems Thinking as a mental model. I created it as a Claude Skill[^2], so that it can be added to your Claude environment and always be available for use. (The standard has been adopted by OpenAI and others, as [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/home) so without too much effort, you should be able to use the skill in most LLMs)

Since most people in a workshop don't already have Claude Code running, they just copied my Claude skill text: https://github.com/mlevison/systems-thinking -- specifically this file: references/questions-of-a-systems-thinker.md and put it at the start of their conversations

I also crafted a challenging situation where I thought Systems thinking would help. Let's run with an example here:

<HighlightBox heading="Our Fictional Problem" variant="caseStudy">
## Case Study: Horizontally Stratified Teams
A senior architect is trapped in what he calls a "vicious death spiral." His project connects to dozens of external systems, and the Scrum Master decided to split the work: one team handles user stories while another manages technical integrations. Six sprints in, refinement and planning sessions routinely exceed eight hours. Stories arrive incomplete, missing critical integration details. The technical team launches into deep dives the story team can't follow. Meanwhile, the story team keeps surfacing requirements that expose unexpected integration challenges. Dependencies bounce between groups, estimates become guesswork, and team members mentally check out around hour five.

The architect has watched the same story carry over three sprints because the slicing never works. The Scrum Master keeps extending sessions, believing more time will surface all hidden complexity. The architect is convinced there must be a way to groom, slice, and size stories in under ten minutes. He just can't see how to get there from here.
</HighlightBox>
As usual with a GenAI model, the conversation is long. I'm excerpting key details and then sharing my response.
> Let me start with a foundational question: What organizational forces or constraints led to the decision to horizontally stratify teams in the first place?

**My response:** In the past, before Scrum, the whole stratified by specialized teams. Since Scrum has come in, nothing has changed. Everyone says it is just more efficient.
> The phrase "everyone says it is just more efficient" is particularly telling—it points to an unexamined mental model that may be creating a self-reinforcing loop.
> ...
> Question for you: When people say "it's more efficient," what evidence are they using? Are they measuring:
> - Individual utilization rates? (people staying busy in their specialty)
> - Or actual throughput of completed, valuable features to customers?

**My response:** They're measuring how much work (output) each person gets done.
> There it is. This is a classic systems thinking trap called local optimization at the expense of global optimization. The organization is measuring output (how busy each specialist is) but not outcome (how quickly customer value flows through the system).
>...
> What's happening to the people in this system? You mentioned team members "checking out mentally around hour five." What are you observing in terms of morale, turnover, or people's sense of effectiveness?

**My response:** At the start of each big release people are enthusiastic. As release wears on, priorities change and the pressure to get everything done increases.

<CalloutBox heading="The following was the most insightful element of the whole exchange">
>The system keeps trying to solve a structure problem with a process problem.
>
>**Question for you**:
> When a release ends—does the organization do retrospectives or post-mortems? And if so, what explanations do people give for why things took longer than expected?
> Do they say:
> - "Requirements weren't clear enough"
> - "We didn't plan well enough"
>- "The technology was more complex than we thought"
>
> Or do they ever say:
>  - "Our team structure creates coordination overhead we're not accounting for"?
</CalloutBox>
**My response:** They tend to comment on the requirements because that is another department.

## Visualizing Problems with Causal Loop Diagrams
This could go on forever, and the [conversation was already over 300 lines](/sample-systems-thinking-conversation/), so I asked: "Before we go any further, let's visualize what we have so far with a Causal Loop diagram". Diagrams in the Markdown world are typically done with Mermaid (what a name), and so I rendered them with the free Mermaid editor
<Figure
  src={CLDForHorizontalTeam}
  alt="Causal Loop Diagram showing local optimization trap in horizontally stratified Scrum teams"
  caption="Causal Loop Diagram showing local optimization trap in horizontally stratified Scrum teams"
  align='right'
/>

This picture illustrates some of the key challenges in the conversation and would make a good starting point for further conversation.
## Conclusion: Using GenAI for Deeper Team Analysis
Be careful of taking the outputs of the model too seriously, remember its only job is to predict the next most likely token, it has no understanding. In addition, if you read the [much longer version of the conversation](/sample-systems-thinking-conversation/), you will see the model made a few logical leaps that would need to be checked.

## Systems Thinking a Claude Skill
The skill is found in the repo: [Systems Thinking Skill for Claude Code](https://github.com/mlevison/systems-thinking). Please Github issues to make suggestions.

## Conclusion: Using GenAI for Deeper Team Analysis
Systems Thinking is most helpful when it is part of a conversation among a group working on a problem together. It is a tool that helps build a shared understanding of the world. The intention of this skill is to make it easier to have those conversations and to ask questions that might have been missed. Please use this with others and not in isolation.

[^1]: Waters Centre Systems Thinking Cards: https://thinkingtoolsstudio.waterscenterst.org/cards
[^2]: Claude Skills are specialized instruction sets that teach Claude how to excel at specific tasks - like creating professional documents, building presentations, or analyzing systems. A big benefit is that skills are only loaded into Claude's working memory when needed. So our Systems Thinking skill sits in the background, and Claude will pull it in when your conversation calls for it. This saves on tokens and makes it's use more efficient.

<LinkList heading = "Related Blog Entries">
    - Systems Thinking is much more useful than [AI Chatbots for Agile Coaches: Why They Fail](/blog/ai-chatbots-for-agile-coaches-why-they-fail/)
    - [GenAI and the Feature Factory: Automating Away Collaboration](/blog/gen-ai-and-the-feature-factory-automating-away-collaboration/) - a systems problem where local optimization harms the whole
    - [Agile Bonuses - The Damage They Do](/blog/agile-bonuses-the-damage-they-do/) - is an example of Systems Thinking
    - [Scrum Anti-Patterns: Micromanagement](/blog/scrum-anti-patterns-micromanagement/)
    - [Hidden Complexity Tax: How It Kills Organizational Resilience](/blog/how-hidden-complexity-tax-saps-organization-resilience/)
    - [Canada's AI Strategy Mistakes Adoption for Productivity](/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/) - Systems Thinking applied to healthcare bottlenecks
</LinkList>

3	date: '2023-11-23'
