9	excerpt: '_Scrum team **Working Agreements** are a simple, powerful way of creating explicit'
10	---
11	
12	import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro'
13	import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
14	import APRBlogIllustrationsAug2019ScrumByExampleWorkingAgreementsV2A from 'images/APR_Blog-Illustrations_Aug2019_ScrumByExample_WorkingAgreements_v2-A.jpg';
15	import APRBlogIllustrationsAug2019ScrumByExampleWorkingAgreementsV2B from 'images/APR_Blog-Illustrations_Aug2019_ScrumByExample_WorkingAgreements_v2-B.jpg';
16	
17	<Figure
18	  src={APRBlogIllustrationsAug2019ScrumByExampleWorkingAgreementsV2A}
19	  alt="Team Friction? Working Agreements may be the solution you need."
20	  caption="Team Friction? Working Agreements may be the solution you need."
21	/>
22	
23	
24	_Scrum team **Working Agreements** are a simple, powerful way of creating explicit guidelines for what kind of work culture you want for your Team. They are a reminder for everyone about how they can commit to respectful behaviour and communication. In this post we'll see how the fictional World's Smallest Online Bookstore (WSOBS) Scrum team struggles without a Working Agreement, and why having one would be useful._
25	
26	Acceptance Criteria
27	
28	<HighlightBox heading="Dramatis Personae" variant="caseStudy">
29	**Steve:** - A scrumMaster and the hero of our story
30	
31	**Paula:** - The Product Owner of Steve's team
32	
33	**Kirby** – one of the Team's software developers
34	
35	**Tonia** – the Team's Quality Assurance specialist
36	
37	**Doug** – another of the Team's software developers
38	
39	**Ian** – the Team's Business Logic programming specialist
40	</HighlightBox>
41	
42	In the past few Sprints, there have been moments of social friction noticed by both Steve and the rest of the WSOBS Team. They included:
43	
44	Kirby was blunt when discussing a defect with both Tonia and Ian.
45	
46	Some discussions with the whole Team became so heated that the quieter team members stopped speaking up for several days.
47	
48	Doug was late for Daily Scrum on several days.
49	
50	On multiple occasions, Team members needed to ask Paula some questions, but she wasn't available by email, and they often didn't know how to find her.
51	
52	None of these individual issues was truly bad, however, taken together and left unchecked, they harm the Team's cohesion. When that happens, people opt to stay silent when there is an opportunity to share an opinion, and events like Daily Scrum becomes less useful when Team members signal their disrespect by frequently being late.
53	
54	During the next Retrospective, Steve mentions a few of these issues and says that he wants to talk about making their environment better. Tonia shares that she knows another one of their peer teams has created their own Working Agreement to reduce some of the friction and improve respect.
55	
56	Before we see how Steve helps his team in this episode, let's make sure we understand what a Working Agreement is, and should be.
57	
58	## What is a Working Agreement?
59	
60	A Working Agreement is a short set of guidelines created by the Scrum Team, that establishes what the expectations of the team members are for one another. A well-written Agreement should help establish and reinforce a clear, shared understanding about what team members agree is good behaviour and communication.
61	
62	## Why do Working Agreements Matter?
63	
64	Working Agreements help make implicit social expectations explicit. (Whoa, that's a mouthful.) They invite team members to tell each other what matters to them on a whole host of topics. This leads to a shared understanding and, in return, a reduction in friction. Done well, they also invite open and honest communication which helps create psychological safety.
65	
66	## Characteristics of an Effective Scrum Team Working Agreement
67	
68	A Working Agreement doesn't have a police force to ensure that it's followed. Its effectiveness comes from being:
69	
70	- **Public and Visible** – preferably written in a large font and posted in a prominent space (perhaps where Daily Stand-up takes place)
71	- **Collaborative** – created by all, not imposed by others
72	- **Short** – a small list of agreements that are easily remembered and lived up to trumps a big list that overwhelms people and gets forgotten
73	- **Updated Frequently** – [Taiichi Ohno](https://blog.gembaacademy.com/2010/02/16/excerpts_from_an_interview_with_taiichi_ohno_july_1/) once said: "If the kanbans do not change for one month, you are salary thieves"
74	- **Consequential** – when the agreements are violated, Team members call out the violation with respectful reminders
75	
76	## Working Agreements Should be Unique to Team Needs
77	Each Scrum Team will create its own Working Agreement based on the context of its work. Elements of an Agreement might include some of these examples:
78	
79	- **Core hours** – times during the day that all Team members agree to be present and available for collaboration.
80	- **Daily Standup** – the time that it happens.
81	- **Attendance** for meetings or events – whether or not you agree to support decisions made. in your absence, whether you will let your team know in advance if you can't attend.
82	- **Product Owner** – availability and contact information.
83	- **Definition of Done** - an agreement about quality
84	- How the Team **limits Work in Progress**.
85	- How the Team ensures everyone has an **equal voice** and feels respected. For example, use of a talking stick, where the person who has the stick has the opportunity to talk and everyone else focuses on them. My favorite tool is a bean bag or ball that can easily be tossed from person to person, rather than a stick.
86	- **Decision-Making** Process and Rules - establish a clear process for making decisions: consensus-based decision-making or voting mechanisms as needed. (See [Why Group Decision-Making Techniques are Important](/blog/why-are-group-decision-making-techniques-important/) for more depth.)
87	- **Skill development** – maybe it's agreed that during each Sprint at least one Team Member will work on growing a skill outside of their core strengths.
88	- **Technical Debt** - in the case of software development, maybe there's an element that states every Sprint the Team will make an effort to improve some part of their codebase.
89	- **Impediments** - Guidelines for handling them.
90	- An understanding of how to resolve **conflict** – for example, ask for a facilitator, or echo back your understanding of the other person's viewpoint, etc.
91	- **Handling Outside Interruptions** - define procedures for managing interruptions during the Sprint itself, such as setting expectations with stakeholders and limiting distractions within the team.
92	- **Sustainable Pace** - how can the team ensure that they're committing to work that is realistically achievable in the Sprint?
93	- **Team Values** - review the Scrum Values and decide how they apply in your world. As a reminder, the Scrum Values are "Focus, Commitment, Courage, Openness and Respect". Many teams also discuss topics that include collaboration, continuous learning, and customer focus.
94	- **Communication Channels** - agree on preferred communication channels (e.g. Slack, Microsoft Teams) for day-to-day interactions and set expectations around response times. (_Hint: instant response is unhealthy._)
95	- **Collaboration Tools** - choose appropriate tools (e.g. Mural, Miro) to facilitate team collaboration and ensure everyone has access to them.
96	- **Celebrating Successes** - how will the team celebrate successes?
97	- **Handling Disagreements** - establish protocols for addressing disagreements within the team.
98	- **Violations of Working Agreements** - define a simple rule on how to point out when someone breaks the working agreements.
99	
100	### Co-located teams might have working agreements for:
101	- **Cell phones** – if or when it is appropriate to use them during Team events.
102	- **Headphones** – when it is fine to use headphones, versus when Team members will not use them so they're available to communicate and collaborate with others.
103	
104	### Remote teams might consider:
105	- Use of **cameras** in online meetings - establish guidelines around camera usage. (_Hint: collaboration is more effective when our cameras are on where possible._)
106	- Commitment not to use other tools (email, chat, phone, …) during team events.
107	
108	### Hybrid teams:
109	- The day(s) of the Sprint that all team members commit to being in the office (_Hint: where practical, Sprint Planning, Review and Retrospective are more effective in person_.)
110	- How to include remote team members in a meeting when half the team is in the office and the other half is online.
111	
112	## Working Agreements and Scrum Values
113	As part of a team coming up with their own list of elements to have in their Working Agreement, it is worth considering the Scrum Values as a source of guidance:
114	
115	- **Focus**: Because we focus on only a few things at a time, we work well together and produce excellent work. We deliver valuable items sooner.
116	- **Courage**: Because we are not alone, we feel supported and have more resources at our disposal. This gives us the courage to undertake greater challenges.
117	- **Openness**: As we work together, we practice expressing how we're doing, and what's in our way. We learn that it is good to express concerns so that they can be addressed.
118	- **Commitment**: Because we have great control over our own destiny, we become more committed to success.
119	- **Respect**: As we work together, sharing successes and failures, we come to respect each other, and to help each other become worthy of respect.
120	
121	Teams normally create a Working Agreement before their first Sprint by setting aside an hour or two beforehand. In the case of our fictional World's Smallest Online Bookstore (WSOB) Team, they haven't yet. No time like the present!
122	
123	### How To Build a Scrum Team Working Agreement - How Can a ScrumMaster Help?
124	Sensing the atmosphere of the Team, Steve starts by helping them learn about Working Agreements. He first ensures that the Team understands what Working Agreements are, and how they will personally benefit from having them.
125	
126	_Mark's note: Spending some time on a good setup will reduce cynicism among Team members. Giving people some categories or areas in which Working Agreements will help, gives them a framework. For instance, [in our workshops](#workshops), categories are cell phones, laptops, break times, and punctuality. In the context of a Team, you might use some of the areas mentioned above, and perhaps draw on the Scrum Values, but ultimately the Team chooses what works best for them._
127	
128	Steve then facilitates a Retrospective to help the Team and Product Owner come together to sort out some of their problems. During the process, they discuss the friction they have felt over the previous few Sprints. They agree to create a Working Agreement and, since it will likely take over an hour, they elect to make it an action item for the next Sprint Retrospective.
129	
130	_There isn't an official or correct way to create Working Agreements, so Steve uses the approach that I share in my workshops. As usual for a ScrumMaster, good preparation pays dividends. Consider canvassing the Team beforehand about categories/areas for agreement._
131	
132	## Facilitating the Creation of a Working Agreement
133	
134	### Check-In
135	As with Retrospectives, asking check-in questions helps to give team members an opportunity to engage with the purpose (in this case, create a Working Agreement) and to understand what might have your teammates worried or preoccupied. Try using a round-robin format, where each person speaks one-on-one with everyone else, in turn.
136	
137	Some opening questions you might use:
138	- What has your attention today?
139	- What keeps you up at night?
140	- How would you describe where your head is? And your heart?
141	- What are you grateful for?
142	- How are you feeling today?
143	
144	Once we've established where our teammates are at as people, we can move on to crafting the working agreements proper.
145	
146	### Coach, But Don't Lead
147	Use prompt questions such as the following examples to help the group craft their Working Agreement:
148	
149	- "What are the decisions that, if made now, could help us in the future when the pressure is on, or things haven't gone our way?[^1]
150	- How do we envision our interactions and behaviours?
151	- What are our shared values and principles?
152	- How do we handle conflict and challenges?
153	- How do we hold each other accountable?
154	- How do we uphold these working agreements?
155	
156	Get everyone to answer. Explain the format you will use and any ground rules that you have in place.  For example, you might have ground rules:
157	
158	- Assume positive intent
159	- If you say 'no' to a proposed item, you're expected to try to make it better.
160	- Use the Decider Protocol: Thumbs Up – I'm good; Sideways – I can live with it; Thumbs down – I will block this proposal. (see: Core Protocols for more depth)
161	
162	Break groups larger than five people into sub-groups. _In my experience, it's easier to get small group agreement first, then bring it back to the whole._
163	
164	Invite the small groups to create a potential Working Agreement in each area or category. Invite them to create any additional Working Agreements they feel are needed to address concerns or conflicts.
165	
166	At the end of 5-10 minutes, get the groups back together and review the proposed items.
167	
168	After a couple of rounds of proposals, if there isn't any consensus on a particular item, move on —they can't establish an agreement in that area for now. Consider revisiting the item the next time Working Agreements get deliberated.
169	
170	Every few Sprints, the Working Agreement should be updated, often by checking it in Retrospective and asking a question like, "Are these still our working agreements? What would we like to update? What areas need new agreements?"
171	
172	After talking to Team members, Steve selects "Daily Scrum Start Time," "Respect," "Phone usage in Team Events," and "How to give everyone equal voice for discussion" as elements to include in the Working Agreement. He explains that if there are other categories that the Team would like to consider including in the Working Agreement, they're welcome to add them as they go.
173	
174	Given the previous friction between some Team members, he opts for a 1-2-4 model[^2] for discussing possible agreements. This model is designed to ensure that everyone has a voice in the process:
175	
176	- Each Team member (1) takes a few minutes to share to the whole group their ideas for potential agreements in each category.
177	- They then work in pairs (2) to record the best ideas from each person. As facilitator, Steve is paying attention to the conversations and outcomes. It should be a red flag if one person is dominating their partner during this step.
178	- Next, they move to groups of four (4) to further consolidate their ideas and present them to the group for discussion. In the case of Steve's Team, there are only six people, so they skip this step and move straight to final group consensus.
179	
180	Steve starts asking for proposed agreements in their first area of focus: Daily Scrum Start Time. After each potential working agreement, he uses the Decider Protocol to check for consensus rapidly. When there isn't immediate consensus, the person who said 'no' to an idea suggests what they think is a better one. If multiple people have an issue, then each is expected to offer a better idea. If too many people say no, then the proposer should consider withdrawing the proposal.
181	
182	In the case of Steve's World's Smallest Online Book Store Team, after 20 minutes, the team have their first set of Working Agreements:
183	
184	- Respect – when another Team member is talking, don't interrupt. When they've finished, pause, reflect, and share back your understanding of their idea.[^3]
185	
186	- Make sure everyone has a voice – more vocal Team members volunteer to speak last to give quieter Team members an opportunity to speak up.
187	
188	- Daily Scrum is 9:20 am, allowing all Team members to get their kids to school before coming in to work.
189	
190	- Cellphones in Team Events – they stay outside the room.
191	
192	- To improve the quality of all ideas, we encourage respectful dissent. At least one Team member volunteers to be the dissenter. Even if they think the original idea is good, they're expected to find criticisms of the idea with the goal of making it stronger.[^4]
193	
194	- Focus – during the Sprint, the Team is focused on the Sprint Goal. If something comes up that doesn't fit the goal, Team Members are expected to say no.
195	
196	_Notice that the last two items weren't among those previously suggested by Steve, instead, they appeared organically. For more on how psychological safety and collaboration contribute to team effectiveness, see [Characteristics of Effective Scrum Teams](/blog/characteristics-of-effective-scrum-teams/)._
197	
198	Steve then offers a suggestion of his own: "If you miss a meeting/event it is expected that you will support the decisions made there." Kirby, who has previous experience facilitating, reminded Steve that if he truly is playing the role of facilitator as part of his ScrumMaster duties, then he is expected to remain neutral and not inject his own ideas.
199	
200	<Figure
201	  src={APRBlogIllustrationsAug2019ScrumByExampleWorkingAgreementsV2B}
202	  alt="Working Agreements - the solution to create the work culture you want for your team."
203	  caption="Working Agreements - the solution to create the work culture you want for your team."
204	/>
205	
206	
207	The Team compiles all the individual agreements in the Working Agreement and posts it on the Team room wall. In the months afterwards, Team members slowly get used to the idea of reminding their peers of behaviours that don't honour the Agreement. Every few Sprints, Steve asks in a Retrospective "Is this still our Working Agreement? Is there anything you would like to change?" The list evolves as Team members find more areas where they see benefits. After six months, they find themselves much better able to deal with tense problems within the Team, or when the outside pressure increases on them.
208	
209	_**[Scrum by Example](/blog/category/scrum-by-example/) is a narrative-style blog series designed to help people new to Scrum, especially new ScrumMasters. If you are new to the series, we recommend you [check out the introduction](/blog/category/scrum-by-example/) to learn more about the series and discover other helpful articles.**_
210	
211	## Want to learn how to put together really effective Working Agreements?
212	
213	If there is one idea at the heart of Scrum and Agile that is most important, it is respecting the people you work with. When you empower teams to make decisions about how they work, you use one of the most powerful methods to help them be more effective and become high-performing. Working Agreements are a great step toward that improvement. In our Certified ScrumMaster workshops, attendees discover how to support and facilitate these kinds of agreements. If you are committed to helping create a respectful environment for your team, we invite you to [join us to learn how and to gain practical, hands-on experience](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/).
214	
215	[^1]: [https://nomad8.com/articles/creating-working-agreements-that-are-actually-useful](https://nomad8.com/articles/creating-working-agreements-that-are-actually-useful)
216	[^2]: [https://www.liberatingstructures.com/1-1-2-4-all/](https://www.liberatingstructures.com/1-1-2-4-all/)
217	[^3]: [https://agilelearninglabs.com/2008/03/active-listening-techniques/](https://agilelearninglabs.com/2008/03/active-listening-techniques/)
218	[^4]: [https://whatsthepont.com/2011/08/14/ritual-dissent-getting-better-proposals-and-dealing-with-saboteurs/](https://whatsthepont.com/2011/08/14/ritual-dissent-getting-better-proposals-and-dealing-with-saboteurs/)
219

None of these individual issues was truly bad, however, taken together and left unchecked, they harm the Team's cohesion. When that happens, people opt to stay silent when there is an opportunity to share an opinion, and events like Daily Scrum becomes less useful when Team members signal their disrespect by frequently being late.

During the next Retrospective, Steve mentions a few of these issues and says that he wants to talk about making their environment better. Tonia shares that she knows another one of their peer teams has created their own Working Agreement to reduce some of the friction and improve respect.

Before we see how Steve helps his team in this episode, let's make sure we understand what a Working Agreement is, and should be.

## What is a Working Agreement?

A Working Agreement is a short set of guidelines created by the Scrum Team, that establishes what the expectations of the team members are for one another. A well-written Agreement should help establish and reinforce a clear, shared understanding about what team members agree is good behaviour and communication.

## Why do Working Agreements Matter?

Working Agreements help make implicit social expectations explicit. (Whoa, that's a mouthful.) They invite team members to tell each other what matters to them on a whole host of topics. This leads to a shared understanding and, in return, a reduction in friction. Done well, they also invite open and honest communication which helps create psychological safety.

## Characteristics of an Effective Scrum Team Working Agreement

A Working Agreement doesn't have a police force to ensure that it's followed. Its effectiveness comes from being:

- **Public and Visible** – preferably written in a large font and posted in a prominent space (perhaps where Daily Stand-up takes place)
- **Collaborative** – created by all, not imposed by others
- **Short** – a small list of agreements that are easily remembered and lived up to trumps a big list that overwhelms people and gets forgotten
- **Updated Frequently** – [Taiichi Ohno](https://blog.gembaacademy.com/2010/02/16/excerpts_from_an_interview_with_taiichi_ohno_july_1/) once said: "If the kanbans do not change for one month, you are salary thieves"
- **Consequential** – when the agreements are violated, Team members call out the violation with respectful reminders

## Working Agreements Should be Unique to Team Needs
Each Scrum Team will create its own Working Agreement based on the context of its work. Elements of an Agreement might include some of these examples:

- **Core hours** – times during the day that all Team members agree to be present and available for collaboration.
- **Daily Standup** – the time that it happens.
- **Attendance** for meetings or events – whether or not you agree to support decisions made. in your absence, whether you will let your team know in advance if you can't attend.
- **Product Owner** – availability and contact information.
- **Definition of Done** - an agreement about quality
- How the Team **limits Work in Progress**.
- How the Team ensures everyone has an **equal voice** and feels respected. For example, use of a talking stick, where the person who has the stick has the opportunity to talk and everyone else focuses on them. My favorite tool is a bean bag or ball that can easily be tossed from person to person, rather than a stick.
- **Decision-Making** Process and Rules - establish a clear process for making decisions: consensus-based decision-making or voting mechanisms as needed. (See [Why Group Decision-Making Techniques are Important](/blog/why-are-group-decision-making-techniques-important/) for more depth.)
- **Skill development** – maybe it's agreed that during each Sprint at least one Team Member will work on growing a skill outside of their core strengths.
- **Technical Debt** - in the case of software development, maybe there's an element that states every Sprint the Team will make an effort to improve some part of their codebase.
- **Impediments** - Guidelines for handling them.
- An understanding of how to resolve **conflict** – for example, ask for a facilitator, or echo back your understanding of the other person's viewpoint, etc.
- **Handling Outside Interruptions** - define procedures for managing interruptions during the Sprint itself, such as setting expectations with stakeholders and limiting distractions within the team.
- **Sustainable Pace** - how can the team ensure that they're committing to work that is realistically achievable in the Sprint?
- **Team Values** - review the Scrum Values and decide how they apply in your world. As a reminder, the Scrum Values are "Focus, Commitment, Courage, Openness and Respect". Many teams also discuss topics that include collaboration, continuous learning, and customer focus.
- **Communication Channels** - agree on preferred communication channels (e.g. Slack, Microsoft Teams) for day-to-day interactions and set expectations around response times. (_Hint: instant response is unhealthy._)
- **Collaboration Tools** - choose appropriate tools (e.g. Mural, Miro) to facilitate team collaboration and ensure everyone has access to them.
- **Celebrating Successes** - how will the team celebrate successes?
- **Handling Disagreements** - establish protocols for addressing disagreements within the team.
- **Violations of Working Agreements** - define a simple rule on how to point out when someone breaks the working agreements.

### Co-located teams might have working agreements for:
- **Cell phones** – if or when it is appropriate to use them during Team events.
- **Headphones** – when it is fine to use headphones, versus when Team members will not use them so they're available to communicate and collaborate with others.

### Remote teams might consider:
- Use of **cameras** in online meetings - establish guidelines around camera usage. (_Hint: collaboration is more effective when our cameras are on where possible._)
- Commitment not to use other tools (email, chat, phone, …) during team events.

### Hybrid teams:
- The day(s) of the Sprint that all team members commit to being in the office (_Hint: where practical, Sprint Planning, Review and Retrospective are more effective in person_.)
- How to include remote team members in a meeting when half the team is in the office and the other half is online.

## Working Agreements and Scrum Values
As part of a team coming up with their own list of elements to have in their Working Agreement, it is worth considering the Scrum Values as a source of guidance:

- **Focus**: Because we focus on only a few things at a time, we work well together and produce excellent work. We deliver valuable items sooner.
- **Courage**: Because we are not alone, we feel supported and have more resources at our disposal. This gives us the courage to undertake greater challenges.
- **Openness**: As we work together, we practice expressing how we're doing, and what's in our way. We learn that it is good to express concerns so that they can be addressed.
- **Commitment**: Because we have great control over our own destiny, we become more committed to success.
- **Respect**: As we work together, sharing successes and failures, we come to respect each other, and to help each other become worthy of respect.

Teams normally create a Working Agreement before their first Sprint by setting aside an hour or two beforehand. In the case of our fictional World's Smallest Online Bookstore (WSOB) Team, they haven't yet. No time like the present!

### How To Build a Scrum Team Working Agreement - How Can a ScrumMaster Help?
Sensing the atmosphere of the Team, Steve starts by helping them learn about Working Agreements. He first ensures that the Team understands what Working Agreements are, and how they will personally benefit from having them.

_Mark's note: Spending some time on a good setup will reduce cynicism among Team members. Giving people some categories or areas in which Working Agreements will help, gives them a framework. For instance, [in our workshops](#workshops), categories are cell phones, laptops, break times, and punctuality. In the context of a Team, you might use some of the areas mentioned above, and perhaps draw on the Scrum Values, but ultimately the Team chooses what works best for them._

Steve then facilitates a Retrospective to help the Team and Product Owner come together to sort out some of their problems. During the process, they discuss the friction they have felt over the previous few Sprints. They agree to create a Working Agreement and, since it will likely take over an hour, they elect to make it an action item for the next Sprint Retrospective.

_There isn't an official or correct way to create Working Agreements, so Steve uses the approach that I share in my workshops. As usual for a ScrumMaster, good preparation pays dividends. Consider canvassing the Team beforehand about categories/areas for agreement._

## Facilitating the Creation of a Working Agreement

### Check-In
As with Retrospectives, asking check-in questions helps to give team members an opportunity to engage with the purpose (in this case, create a Working Agreement) and to understand what might have your teammates worried or preoccupied. Try using a round-robin format, where each person speaks one-on-one with everyone else, in turn.

Some opening questions you might use:
- What has your attention today?
- What keeps you up at night?
- How would you describe where your head is? And your heart?
- What are you grateful for?
- How are you feeling today?

Once we've established where our teammates are at as people, we can move on to crafting the working agreements proper.

### Coach, But Don't Lead
Use prompt questions such as the following examples to help the group craft their Working Agreement:

- "What are the decisions that, if made now, could help us in the future when the pressure is on, or things haven't gone our way?[^1]
- How do we envision our interactions and behaviours?
- What are our shared values and principles?
- How do we handle conflict and challenges?
- How do we hold each other accountable?
- How do we uphold these working agreements?

Get everyone to answer. Explain the format you will use and any ground rules that you have in place.  For example, you might have ground rules:

- Assume positive intent
- If you say 'no' to a proposed item, you're expected to try to make it better.
- Use the Decider Protocol: Thumbs Up – I'm good; Sideways – I can live with it; Thumbs down – I will block this proposal. (see: Core Protocols for more depth)

Break groups larger than five people into sub-groups. _In my experience, it's easier to get small group agreement first, then bring it back to the whole._

Invite the small groups to create a potential Working Agreement in each area or category. Invite them to create any additional Working Agreements they feel are needed to address concerns or conflicts.

At the end of 5-10 minutes, get the groups back together and review the proposed items.

After a couple of rounds of proposals, if there isn't any consensus on a particular item, move on —they can't establish an agreement in that area for now. Consider revisiting the item the next time Working Agreements get deliberated.

Every few Sprints, the Working Agreement should be updated, often by checking it in Retrospective and asking a question like, "Are these still our working agreements? What would we like to update? What areas need new agreements?"

After talking to Team members, Steve selects "Daily Scrum Start Time," "Respect," "Phone usage in Team Events," and "How to give everyone equal voice for discussion" as elements to include in the Working Agreement. He explains that if there are other categories that the Team would like to consider including in the Working Agreement, they're welcome to add them as they go.

Given the previous friction between some Team members, he opts for a 1-2-4 model[^2] for discussing possible agreements. This model is designed to ensure that everyone has a voice in the process:

- Each Team member (1) takes a few minutes to share to the whole group their ideas for potential agreements in each category.
- They then work in pairs (2) to record the best ideas from each person. As facilitator, Steve is paying attention to the conversations and outcomes. It should be a red flag if one person is dominating their partner during this step.
- Next, they move to groups of four (4) to further consolidate their ideas and present them to the group for discussion. In the case of Steve's Team, there are only six people, so they skip this step and move straight to final group consensus.

Steve starts asking for proposed agreements in their first area of focus: Daily Scrum Start Time. After each potential working agreement, he uses the Decider Protocol to check for consensus rapidly. When there isn't immediate consensus, the person who said 'no' to an idea suggests what they think is a better one. If multiple people have an issue, then each is expected to offer a better idea. If too many people say no, then the proposer should consider withdrawing the proposal.

In the case of Steve's World's Smallest Online Book Store Team, after 20 minutes, the team have their first set of Working Agreements:

- Respect – when another Team member is talking, don't interrupt. When they've finished, pause, reflect, and share back your understanding of their idea.[^3]

- Make sure everyone has a voice – more vocal Team members volunteer to speak last to give quieter Team members an opportunity to speak up.

- Daily Scrum is 9:20 am, allowing all Team members to get their kids to school before coming in to work.

- Cellphones in Team Events – they stay outside the room.

- To improve the quality of all ideas, we encourage respectful dissent. At least one Team member volunteers to be the dissenter. Even if they think the original idea is good, they're expected to find criticisms of the idea with the goal of making it stronger.[^4]

- Focus – during the Sprint, the Team is focused on the Sprint Goal. If something comes up that doesn't fit the goal, Team Members are expected to say no.

_Notice that the last two items weren't among those previously suggested by Steve, instead, they appeared organically. For more on how psychological safety and collaboration contribute to team effectiveness, see [Characteristics of Effective Scrum Teams](/blog/characteristics-of-effective-scrum-teams/)._

Steve then offers a suggestion of his own: "If you miss a meeting/event it is expected that you will support the decisions made there." Kirby, who has previous experience facilitating, reminded Steve that if he truly is playing the role of facilitator as part of his ScrumMaster duties, then he is expected to remain neutral and not inject his own ideas.

<Figure
  src={APRBlogIllustrationsAug2019ScrumByExampleWorkingAgreementsV2B}
  alt="Working Agreements - the solution to create the work culture you want for your team."
  caption="Working Agreements - the solution to create the work culture you want for your team."
/>


The Team compiles all the individual agreements in the Working Agreement and posts it on the Team room wall. In the months afterwards, Team members slowly get used to the idea of reminding their peers of behaviours that don't honour the Agreement. Every few Sprints, Steve asks in a Retrospective "Is this still our Working Agreement? Is there anything you would like to change?" The list evolves as Team members find more areas where they see benefits. After six months, they find themselves much better able to deal with tense problems within the Team, or when the outside pressure increases on them.

_**[Scrum by Example](/blog/category/scrum-by-example/) is a narrative-style blog series designed to help people new to Scrum, especially new ScrumMasters. If you are new to the series, we recommend you [check out the introduction](/blog/category/scrum-by-example/) to learn more about the series and discover other helpful articles.**_

## Want to learn how to put together really effective Working Agreements?

If there is one idea at the heart of Scrum and Agile that is most important, it is respecting the people you work with. When you empower teams to make decisions about how they work, you use one of the most powerful methods to help them be more effective and become high-performing. Working Agreements are a great step toward that improvement. In our Certified ScrumMaster workshops, attendees discover how to support and facilitate these kinds of agreements. If you are committed to helping create a respectful environment for your team, we invite you to [join us to learn how and to gain practical, hands-on experience](/courses/certified-scrummaster-csm-training/).

[^1]: [https://nomad8.com/articles/creating-working-agreements-that-are-actually-useful](https://nomad8.com/articles/creating-working-agreements-that-are-actually-useful)
[^2]: [https://www.liberatingstructures.com/1-1-2-4-all/](https://www.liberatingstructures.com/1-1-2-4-all/)
[^3]: [https://agilelearninglabs.com/2008/03/active-listening-techniques/](https://agilelearninglabs.com/2008/03/active-listening-techniques/)
[^4]: [https://whatsthepont.com/2011/08/14/ritual-dissent-getting-better-proposals-and-dealing-with-saboteurs/](https://whatsthepont.com/2011/08/14/ritual-dissent-getting-better-proposals-and-dealing-with-saboteurs/)

21	Here are some elements commonly found in a Definition of Ready:
22	
23	- Clear Understanding. Everyone agrees on what each Backlog Item represents.
24	- Estimated and Small. The item has an estimate and it is, at most, a Small or 1, 2, 3 Story Points.
25	- Acceptance Criteria. All acceptance criteria has been defined.
26	- Dependencies. All dependencies have been discovered.
27	- User Interface. A feature requires a mockup.
28	
29	This list has strong parallels to the INVEST criteria and, as long as it remains a lightweight check, Definition of Ready can be a tool for good.
30	
31	A team with a Definition of Ready isn’t optimizing for getting an idea from entering the Product Backlog to Deployed. Instead, they’re optimizing for Sprint Backlog to Deployed. The Definition of Ready acts a gate between the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Items can be held up at the gate for trivial reasons (e.g. incomplete Acceptance Criteria, missing user interface mockup, etc).

34	  src={DefinitionOfReadyHarmfulHelpfulExamples1024x538}
35	  alt="Scrum Definition of Ready - harmful and helpful examples"

37	/>

40	A rigid Definition of Ready encourages local optimization for the throughput of just the Scrum Team. This sounds like a more positive thing than it really is. The problem is that we should be optimizing for the whole system from the moment the customer places asks for their feature, until it is delivered. A rigid “Ready”, makes the Scrum Team look better by improving their cycle time, without necessarily improving things for the client. Imagine an example where a Definition of Ready holds up a feature for 6+ weeks while requirements are being gathered (perhaps the User Interface details, or final Acceptance criteria). Sure, once the work starts, it proceeds at a normal pace, but now the Scrum Team can say that they’ve reduced their cycle time, when all that really happened is the delay was pushed to early in the system. The team feels good but the customer isn't any happier. The customer's item still spent a long time sitting in a queue, and it doesn't matter what the queue was.
41	
42	For teams that use a Definition of Ready, they should consider measuring Lead Time and not Cycle Time. By measuring Lead Time, any time spent waiting at the Ready gate is accounted for, making it harder to sub-optimize. This also leads to a general principle that says, when measuring, prefer measurements that observe the whole system.

48	/>

Hold on to the definition lightly - it shouldn't be rigid, and everything must 100% compliance check. Instead of making statements like "all acceptance criteria", consider "some or enough acceptance criteria have been found". Instead of a "requires a mockup" element, try "features that require large UI changes check to see if a mockup would help, preferring pencil sketches". Finally, as the team matures, check to see if the Definition of Ready can be made thinner by reducing the number of elements in it. Be careful that this doesn’t become a dumping ground  for every little problem the team ever had.

---

import Figure from '@/components/global/figure.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
import DefinitionOfReadyHarmfulHelpfulExamples1024x538 from '@/content/glossary/definition-of-ready/images/Definition-of-Ready-harmful-helpful-examples-1024x538.jpg';
import LeadTimeCycleTimeKanbanBoardExample from '@/content/glossary/definition-of-ready/images/Lead-time-Cycle-time-kanban-board-example.png';


import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';

**Definition of Ready** is an agreement between the Product Owner and the team that describes what state Product Backlog Items (or User Stories) need to be in before the Sprint. Another way of describing “ready” is how prepared Stories are to be worked on.

A Definition of Ready helps a Scrum (or Kanban) team to ensure that their Product Backlog Items are well thought out, so nothing is considered for Sprint work if it has a high risk of getting stuck because some part of the work was ill-understood.

Here are some elements commonly found in a Definition of Ready:

- Clear Understanding. Everyone agrees on what each Backlog Item represents.
- Estimated and Small. The item has an estimate and it is, at most, a Small or 1, 2, 3 Story Points.
- Acceptance Criteria. All acceptance criteria has been defined.
- Dependencies. All dependencies have been discovered.
- User Interface. A feature requires a mockup.

This list has strong parallels to the INVEST criteria and, as long as it remains a lightweight check, Definition of Ready can be a tool for good.

A team with a Definition of Ready isn’t optimizing for getting an idea from entering the Product Backlog to Deployed. Instead, they’re optimizing for Sprint Backlog to Deployed. The Definition of Ready acts a gate between the Product Backlog and the Sprint Backlog. Items can be held up at the gate for trivial reasons (e.g. incomplete Acceptance Criteria, missing user interface mockup, etc).

<Figure
  src={DefinitionOfReadyHarmfulHelpfulExamples1024x538}
  alt="Scrum Definition of Ready - harmful and helpful examples"
  caption="Scrum Definition of Ready - harmful and helpful examples"
/>


A rigid Definition of Ready encourages local optimization for the throughput of just the Scrum Team. This sounds like a more positive thing than it really is. The problem is that we should be optimizing for the whole system from the moment the customer places asks for their feature, until it is delivered. A rigid “Ready”, makes the Scrum Team look better by improving their cycle time, without necessarily improving things for the client. Imagine an example where a Definition of Ready holds up a feature for 6+ weeks while requirements are being gathered (perhaps the User Interface details, or final Acceptance criteria). Sure, once the work starts, it proceeds at a normal pace, but now the Scrum Team can say that they’ve reduced their cycle time, when all that really happened is the delay was pushed to early in the system. The team feels good but the customer isn't any happier. The customer's item still spent a long time sitting in a queue, and it doesn't matter what the queue was.

For teams that use a Definition of Ready, they should consider measuring Lead Time and not Cycle Time. By measuring Lead Time, any time spent waiting at the Ready gate is accounted for, making it harder to sub-optimize. This also leads to a general principle that says, when measuring, prefer measurements that observe the whole system.

<Figure
  src={LeadTimeCycleTimeKanbanBoardExample}
  alt="Lead time Cycle time kanban board example"
  caption="Lead time Cycle time kanban board example"
/>


My own preference is that, if your team has items that are frequently getting stuck in Sprint, consider a Definition of Ready but only cover the details that are currently causing problems. Hold on to the definition lightly - it shouldn't be rigid, and everything must 100% compliance check. Instead of making statements like "all acceptance criteria", consider "some or enough acceptance criteria have been found". Instead of a "requires a mockup" element, try "features that require large UI changes check to see if a mockup would help, preferring pencil sketches". Finally, as the team matures, check to see if the Definition of Ready can be made thinner by reducing the number of elements in it. Be careful that this doesn’t become a dumping ground  for every little problem the team ever had.

date: '2026-02-05'

---

import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';
import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';

The **Last Responsible Moment** sounds like a fancy name for procrastination, though it isn't. Instead of procrastination, it's about remaining flexible and deciding when we have more information.

A useful framing: think about how much more you'll know about a problem or decision in the future. Is the person sitting here now the same person six weeks from now? Of course, the answer is "future me" will know more. So why lock in a decision today when future-you will be better equipped to make it?

With the Last Responsible Moment, we delay decisions until the cost of not deciding exceeds the benefit of delaying. When we make a decision too early, we bake in the assumptions we were making at the time. When we delay too long, we lose the ability to make the decision altogether.

A practical approach when facing a decision:
- When is the last time I could make this decision?
- What would I need to know before I make this decision?

This idea appears throughout the Agile Universe, even when we don't name it. All Agile Engineering Practices are about avoiding early decisions. In Product Backlog Refinement, we encourage teams only to refine a few Sprints' worth of work. The list goes on.

The idea of the Last Responsible Moment came to the Agile community via Mary and Tom Poppendieck's *Lean Software Development: An Agile Toolkit*:

> Delay commitment until the last responsible moment, that is, the moment at which failing to make a decision eliminates an important alternative.

Not everyone loves the framing: Rebecca Wirfs-Brock argues that we should decide at the “most responsible moment”, the point where we know enough to choose well, rather than nervously delaying until an alternative is about to disappear (see Resource Links below).

---
date: 2026-06-26
subject: "Nearly Trillon Dollar Valuations and GenAI Still Can't Follow Simple Instructons"        # Version A → goes into the draft
---

I think we humans have a great future continuing to do real work. This week has provided good reminders that LLMs have real limitations.

It's amazing how LLMs can quickly go down the wrong path, wasting time and energy. I'm thinking about buying a new bike. It's been 20 years since I last looked seriously so I wanted to understand the state of modern biking technology, e.g. Gravel vs Hybrid vs Touring and everything else that has changed.

Since I wanted depth and not a listicle, I thought I would use Gemini Flash as a search engine. I wrote a prompt covering my current bike and limitations, then what I was looking to read about. I ended the prompt with a specific instruction: "Instead of doing analysis, I want to read long form articles that cover modern bike choices."

What I got back was a detailed analysis that summarized articles. When I asked for links I found I was getting very narrow articles like: [a 2016 post on tire pressure](https://janheine.wordpress.com/2016/03/09/tire-pressure-take-home/) - which might be great reading at the end of my process, not now. (Also 2016 - is this still current? I'll have to check.) If the analysis from Gemini were taken at face value, I would seriously consider hookless rims. I already know the answer is no unless you have very specific needs.

I assumed by asking Flash, it would do less "thinking". I fed the same prompt into Claude Sonnet - set for low effort. I spent my lunchtime reading some very good articles on how gravel bikes perform - far better than 20 year old hybrid.

This isn't about Claude being better than Gemini. I'm more interested from a professional perspective. This is a good reminder. These models are often awful at following instructions.

Gemini was good at summarizing, so when I wanted to build a table of the bikes I'm considering, I gave it the URLs of each specific bike from Ottawa bike shops and asked it to build a table.

The problem is that I knew some of the facts in the table were wrong. After some searching, I think that Gemini had trouble accessing the specific pages. Instead of telling me, it went off and found descriptions of older models.

I'm really hoping the bike fitting I get next week will not involve AI.

## Backlog Refinement Anti-Patterns
I published a blog post: "[How Many of These Backlog Refinement Anti-Patterns Does Your Team Have?](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/how-many-of-these-backlog-refinement-anti-patterns-does-your-team-have/)" and even here an LLM managed to make an interesting mistake.

*Background:* I do my writing in Markdown (Obsidian) and the website is built with Astro (a static site generator that uses MDX - Markdown with JSX).

When a blog post is ready for publishing, I copy the Markdown file into the Astro project. Since there are a number of small formatting differences between Obsidian and Astro (handling of images, callouts, etc.), I have a Claude Skill that is supposed to do the conversion. Claude deleted the file. It had found a rule to check for warnings, found warnings associated with the post and deleted it.

Since it was just operating on a copy of the original Markdown file this didn’t matter.

## Humans still matter
In spite of the continued hype (Anthropic has upped its pre-IPO valuation to nearly $1 trillion), it seems that LLMs are still far from being ready to replace humans on many simple tasks.

This was a big topic of discussion in this week’s Certified Scrum Developer workshop. As a result of the discussion, I did a significant update to the [Agile Architecture Glossary](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/agile-architecture/).

Running a technical workshop is time-consuming and so there isn’t a reading list this week.

## Next Week
Between Canada Day and my regular Quarterly Review, there won’t be a newsletter next week. Let's all take time to enjoy family and friends.

Tell me what your plans are.

Got everything I need. Newsletter pick: the **2026-06-26 "Nearly Trillion-Dollar Valuations / GenAI Still Can't Follow Instructions"** issue (24 days old, unused, strongest skeptical-pragmatist angle of the eligible set).

Here's the plan and the drafts. I read every source in full and each draft is re-cut from your own sentences, connected prose, current length. **Structure:** 4 posting days, each = one substantial piece + one glossary reshare (8 posts total).

- **Day 1:** Canada's AI Strategy (recent, again) + glossary: Product Backlog
- **Day 2:** GenAI + Systems Thinking (recent #2) + glossary: Definition of Ready
- **Day 3:** Team Friction / Working Agreements (older) + glossary: Product Backlog Refinement
- **Day 4:** Newsletter (trillion-dollar / instructions) + glossary: Last Responsible Moment

A/B options for the four main pieces and the two richer glossary entries; a single tight draft for the two thinner glossary definitions. Pick one per slot, tweak in your own hand, and tell me which - I'll build the 3-platform batch JSON.

---

## DAY 1 — Canada's AI Strategy (recent, again)
`/blog/canadas-ai-strategy-mistakes-adoption-for-productivity/`

### Option A — adoption isn't productivity
**Angle:** the core thesis, straight at the strategy's headline number.

Canada has a real productivity problem, and we have for decades. In 1984 the Canadian economy was 88% as productive as the US per hour worked; by 2022 it had fallen to 71%. The new national AI strategy is an attempt to fix that, promising a 3 percent increase in GDP by raising business adoption of GenAI from 12 percent today to 60 percent by 2034.

Here's my worry: adoption of GenAI doesn't make an organization more productive. Dropping GenAI onto a broken process just automates the mess. Worse, a target like this invites AI washing, because when you measure success by adoption rate, organizations will claim they're "doing AI" to hit the number, whether or not anything meaningful changes.

Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn't make it so. If we want to improve productivity, we need to look at each organization as a system, understand the bottlenecks, and focus on eliminating the bottleneck.

What would it take for your organization to measure the outcome instead of the adoption rate?

`#AIinSoftwareDevelopment`

*Source lines:* "Adoption of AI doesn't make an organization more productive." / "dropping AI onto a broken process just automates the mess." / "measure success by adoption rate and organizations will claim they're 'doing AI'." / "Saying a new technology will magically make us more productive doesn't make it so." / closing systems paragraph.

### Option B — the healthcare bottleneck
**Angle:** Humber River Hospital as the concrete example; flow beats "AI".

To make an overflowing emergency room more efficient, we might use GenAI to speed up triage. But if the hospital is already running at 100% or more of its bed capacity, faster triage doesn't help. It lets a handful leave sooner and makes no meaningful difference, because we tackled the emergency room problem in isolation. The beds, our real bottleneck, stay full whether or not triage runs faster.

Humber River Hospital took a different path. Their command centre is staffed by a cross-disciplinary group watching bed allocations, discharge planning, surgical scheduling and critical care capacity, so there's enough knowledge in the room to make good decisions. GE brands it "AI", but the pattern-finding that actually helps predates ChatGPT entirely.

AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective. Predictive analytics is just a tool in this picture.

Before you drop GenAI on a bottleneck, ask whether you've actually studied the flow of the system around it.

*Source lines:* ER triage / bed-capacity passage / command-centre staffing / "AI didn't make Humber River Hospital more effective. Improving the flow in the system made it more effective."

---

## DAY 1 glossary reshare — Product Backlog
`/glossary/product-backlog/`

The Product Backlog is an ordered list of all the work items or value the Product Owner would like to see the team work on in the foreseeable future. Simple enough as a definition. The trouble starts when it stops being ordered and turns into a dumping ground.

An ordered list means someone has decided what matters most, and the team pulls from the top. When everything is "high priority", nothing is, and the list quietly becomes a graveyard of ideas nobody will ever build. A deep backlog isn't a full one; it's one that's well understood near the top and deliberately vague further down, because refining work you may never do is waste.

If your Product Backlog has hundreds of items and no clear order, that's not thoroughness. It's a decision nobody has made yet.

How many items are really in your Product Backlog, and when did you last delete one?

`#Scrum #ProductOwner`

*Source:* the definition line, plus the entry's linked resources ("Make the Product Backlog Deep", "Tips for Reducing the Product Backlog Size").

---

## DAY 2 — GenAI + Systems Thinking (recent #2)
`/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/`

### Option A — the inbox-zero loop
**Angle:** GenAI as a Systems Thinking sparring partner, with the caution attached.

Inbox zero was sold to us by productivity experts, and yet it never seems to happen in real life. When you take a step back, the pattern becomes clear: fast responses to email lead people to learn you get stuff done, which brings more requests into your inbox, which... you get the idea. Without a fancy label, that's Systems Thinking, a mental model that looks at a problem not in isolation but as a series of interconnected parts.

For once, I found a use for GenAI. I've been thinking about how it can aid critical thinking rather than generate more slop, so I built a set of prompts that use Systems Thinking as a mental model and turned them into a Claude Skill. It helps surface the questions I still forget to ask, even after using this lens for years.

One caution: be careful of taking the model's output too seriously. Its only job is to predict the next most likely token; it has no understanding. Systems Thinking is most helpful as part of a conversation among a group working on a problem together, not something you do in isolation.

Where's the feedback loop hiding in a problem your team keeps re-solving?

`#AIinSoftwareDevelopment`

*Source lines:* inbox-zero feedback loop / "For once, I will find a use for GenAI." / "aid critical thinking rather than generate more slop" / "its only job is to predict the next most likely token, it has no understanding" / "Please use this with others and not in isolation."

### Option B — the horizontal-team death spiral
**Angle:** the case study and the local-optimization trap.

A senior architect described his project as a "vicious death spiral." His Scrum Master had split the work: one team handled user stories, another managed technical integrations. Six sprints in, refinement and planning routinely ran past eight hours, stories arrived missing critical integration details, and team members checked out around hour five.

I ran the problem through GenAI as a Systems Thinking sparring partner. The telling moment came when I noted that everyone says the split "is just more efficient". They were measuring how much work each specialist gets done. That's a classic systems thinking trap: local optimization at the expense of global optimization. The organization was measuring output, how busy each specialist is, but not outcome, how quickly customer value flows through the system.

The sharpest line in the whole exchange: the system keeps trying to solve a structure problem with a process problem. The Scrum Master kept extending sessions, believing more time would surface the hidden complexity, when the real issue was the team structure itself.

When your team keeps carrying the same story across sprints, ask whether you're fixing a structure problem with more process.

*Source lines:* case-study text / "local optimization at the expense of global optimization" / "measuring output ... but not outcome" / "The system keeps trying to solve a structure problem with a process problem."

---

## DAY 2 glossary reshare — Definition of Ready
`/glossary/definition-of-ready/`

### Option A — the hidden queue
Definition of Ready is an agreement between the Product Owner and the team about what state a Product Backlog Item needs to be in before it enters a Sprint. Used lightly, it keeps genuinely half-baked work out of the Sprint. Used rigidly, it quietly hurts your customer.

Here's the trap. A rigid Definition of Ready encourages local optimization for the throughput of just the Scrum Team. Imagine an item held at the "Ready" gate for six weeks while requirements are gathered. Once work starts it proceeds at a normal pace, so the team can say they've reduced their cycle time. But all that really happened is the delay moved earlier in the system. The team feels good and the customer isn't any happier, because their item still spent a long time sitting in a queue.

If your team uses a Definition of Ready, measure Lead Time, not Cycle Time. Lead Time counts the waiting at the gate, which makes it much harder to sub-optimize. When you measure, prefer measurements that observe the whole system.

Does your "Ready" gate reduce delay, or just hide it earlier in the process?

`#Scrum`

*Source lines:* "optimizing for Sprint Backlog to Deployed" / rigid-Ready cycle-time passage / "prefer measurements that observe the whole system."

### Option B — hold it lightly
Most teams treat Definition of Ready as a checklist to enforce. I'd rather you hold it lightly.

If items frequently get stuck mid-Sprint because something was ill-understood, a Definition of Ready can help, but only cover the details that are actually causing problems right now. Instead of "all acceptance criteria", try "some or enough acceptance criteria have been found". Instead of "requires a mockup", try "features that need large UI changes check whether a mockup would help, preferring pencil sketches".

Then, as the team matures, check whether the Definition of Ready can be made thinner by reducing the number of elements in it. The failure mode to watch for is that it becomes a dumping ground for every little problem the team ever had. A lightweight check is a tool for good; a rigid gate that everything must 100% comply with is how you end up optimizing for looking productive instead of being useful.

What's one item on your "Ready" checklist that's there because of a problem you had years ago?

`#Scrum #ScrumMaster`

*Source lines:* "only cover the details that are currently causing problems" / "some or enough acceptance criteria" / "pencil sketches" / "dumping ground for every little problem the team ever had."

---

## DAY 3 — Team Friction / Working Agreements (older blog)
`/blog/team-friction-inspires-working-agreements/`

### Option A — friction accumulates
**Angle:** the quiet friction that adds up, and what Working Agreements are for.

On a lot of teams the friction is quiet. Someone's blunt when discussing a defect. A heated discussion leaves the quieter people not speaking up for days. One person is repeatedly late for Daily Scrum. The Product Owner isn't reachable when you have a question.

None of these individual issues is truly bad. But taken together and left unchecked, they harm the team's cohesion, because people opt to stay silent when there's an opportunity to share an opinion, and Daily Scrum becomes less useful when team members signal disrespect by being late.

This is what Working Agreements are for. They make implicit social expectations explicit, inviting team members to tell each other what matters to them. That leads to a shared understanding, a reduction in friction, and open, honest communication that helps create psychological safety.

One caution: a Working Agreement doesn't have a police force. Its effectiveness comes from being public and visible, collaborative rather than imposed, short enough to remember, and updated frequently. When someone breaks it, teammates offer respectful reminders.

What's one piece of quiet friction on your team that's never been said out loud?

`#Scrum #ScrumMaster`

*Source lines:* the friction list / "None of these individual issues was truly bad, however, taken together and left unchecked, they harm the Team's cohesion." / "make implicit social expectations explicit" / the effectiveness characteristics.

### Option B — how to facilitate one
**Angle:** the practical facilitation recipe.

When a team decides to build a Working Agreement, the ScrumMaster's job is to coach, not lead. As usual for a ScrumMaster, good preparation pays dividends, so canvass the team beforehand about the categories that matter: Daily Scrum start time, respect, phone usage in team events, how to give everyone an equal voice.

Start with a check-in, the same as you would in a Retrospective, so people get a chance to say where their head and heart are before the work begins. Then use a format that guarantees every voice is heard. I like the 1-2-4 model: each person shares their ideas, pairs record the best ones, then small groups consolidate and bring proposals back to the whole. Use the Decider Protocol to check for consensus quickly, and when someone says no, they're expected to suggest something better.

Here's what one fictional team landed on: don't interrupt, and reflect back your understanding before responding. More vocal members volunteer to speak last. At least one person volunteers to be the dissenter, expected to find criticisms of an idea with the goal of making it stronger.

Every few Sprints, ask in a Retrospective: is this still our Working Agreement, and what would we like to change?

`#Scrum #ScrumMaster`

## DAY 3 glossary reshare — Product Backlog Refinement
`/glossary/product-backlog-refinement/`

Product Backlog Refinement (once called "grooming") is the session where the whole Scrum Team prepares the Product Backlog for the next few Sprints. New items get added, items too large for one Sprint get broken down, the Product Owner shares the reasoning behind prioritization decisions, and items that no longer matter get deleted to make room.

Notice how much of that is conversation, not paperwork. The value isn't a tidy backlog; it's the shared understanding the team builds while getting there. That's also why I don't think GenAI will speed this event up, and shouldn't. The point of refinement is that a group reaches a common understanding of the work, and you can't outsource that to a tool without losing the very thing you came for.

Which part of refinement does your team treat as paperwork, when it should be a conversation?

`#Scrum`

*Source:* the definition paragraph, plus the entry's linked "Why GenAI won't speed up Backlog Refinement."

## DAY 4 — Newsletter: trillion-dollar valuations / can't follow instructions
2026-06-26 issue. **Link caveat:** newsletters aren't published as individual pages, so the URL drives to `/newsletter-subscribe/` unless you'd rather point at a web-archive of the issue.

### Option A — awful at following instructions
**Angle:** the bike-search example.

I'm thinking about buying a new bike, my first serious look in 20 years, so I wanted to understand how the technology has changed. Since I wanted depth and not a listicle, I tried using an LLM as a search engine. My prompt ended with a specific instruction: "Instead of doing analysis, I want to read long form articles that cover modern bike choices."

What I got back was a detailed analysis that summarized articles. When I asked for links, I got very narrow pieces, including a 2016 post on tire pressure. If I'd taken the analysis at face value, I'd have seriously considered hookless rims, and I already know the answer there is no unless you have very specific needs.

This isn't about one model being better than another. It's a good professional reminder: these models are often awful at following instructions. It's amazing how quickly an LLM can go down the wrong path, wasting time and energy.

In spite of the hype (Anthropic just upped its pre-IPO valuation to nearly $1 trillion), LLMs are still far from ready to replace humans on many simple tasks. I think we humans have a great future continuing to do real work.

Where has an LLM confidently ignored what you actually asked for?

*Source lines:* the bike prompt and instruction / "a detailed analysis that summarized articles" / hookless-rims aside / "these models are often awful at following instructions" / "nearly $1 trillion ... still far from being ready to replace humans on many simple tasks."

### Option B — confidently wrong
**Angle:** the fabricated table + the deleted-file anecdote; the real risk is hidden uncertainty.

GenAI was good at summarizing, so I gave an LLM the URLs of specific bikes from Ottawa bike shops and asked it to build me a comparison table. The problem was that I knew some of the facts in the table were wrong. After some digging, I think the model had trouble accessing the specific pages. Instead of telling me that, it went off and found descriptions of older models and presented them as current.

That's the pattern worth naming: not that the tool made a mistake, but that it filled the gap confidently instead of admitting it couldn't reach the page.

I hit a version of this in my own publishing workflow too. I have a Claude Skill that converts a finished blog post from Obsidian Markdown into the format my website needs. On one run, Claude found a rule to check for warnings, found warnings associated with the post, and deleted the file. It was only operating on a copy, so no harm done, but the instinct is telling.

These tools are genuinely useful, and I couldn't run my business without them. They're also still far from ready to replace humans on many simple tasks. The trick is knowing which is which.

When has an LLM hidden its own uncertainty from you instead of flagging it?

*Source lines:* "I knew some of the facts in the table were wrong" / "Instead of telling me, it went off and found descriptions of older models." / the Claude-deleted-the-file anecdote / "still far from being ready to replace humans on many simple tasks."

## DAY 4 glossary reshare — Last Responsible Moment
`/glossary/last-responsible-moment/`

### Option A — not procrastination
The Last Responsible Moment sounds like a fancy name for procrastination, but it isn't. It's about staying flexible and deciding when you have more information.

Try this framing: think about how much more you'll know about a decision in the future. Is the person sitting here now the same person six weeks from now? Of course not. Future-you will know more, so why lock in a decision today when future-you will be better equipped to make it?

With the Last Responsible Moment, we delay a decision until the cost of not deciding exceeds the benefit of delaying. Make the call too early and you bake in the assumptions you were making at the time. Delay too long and you lose the ability to make the decision at all.

Mary and Tom Poppendieck put it as delaying commitment until the moment at which failing to decide eliminates an important alternative.

What's one decision your team locked in early, only to wish later you'd waited?

`#Agile`

*Source lines:* "sounds like a fancy name for procrastination, though it isn't" / "future me will know more" / "bake in the assumptions ... lose the ability to make the decision altogether" / Poppendieck quote.

### Option B — the "most responsible moment" counterpoint
A quick counterpoint to a favourite Agile idea. The Last Responsible Moment says: delay a decision until failing to make it would eliminate an important alternative. It shows up all over the place. It's why we only refine a few Sprints' worth of work in Product Backlog Refinement, and why good engineering practices avoid early lock-in.

But not everyone loves the framing. Rebecca Wirfs-Brock argues we should decide at the "most responsible moment", the point where we know enough to choose well, rather than nervously delaying until an alternative is about to disappear. I like the tension between the two: "last" keeps you flexible, and "most" keeps you from turning flexibility into brinkmanship.

The practical questions are the same either way: when is the last point I could make this decision, and what would I need to know before I make it?

Are you delaying decisions to stay flexible, or to avoid making them?

`#Agile`

*Source lines:* Poppendieck definition / "This idea appears throughout the Agile Universe ... refine a few Sprints' worth of work" / the Wirfs-Brock "most responsible moment" counter / the two practical questions.

Hi {{ subscriber.first\_name }},

I never imagined that AI would be taking over the world of work. My father often said, "Marvin Minsky promised me AI in 1967, and I'm still waiting". We don't have Minsky's Artificial General Intelligence yet, and despite the sales pitches from OpenAI et al., that doesn't seem likely anytime soon.

  

However, along the way, new and disruptive tools have been created. The ethics and legal issues surrounding these tools are enormous; I would be happy if they didn't exist. Think copyright, energy use, false news stories, slop and deepfakes - just to name a few. Worse, the vendors release new versions, with little consideration for the profound impact they will have.

  

We don't get a say in the training or rollout of these tools; we just have to navigate their impact on our world. I'm not an expert in economics or political systems. I do know something about how organizations work and don't work.

  

We all see the reports in the news about job losses due to GenAI and how, in many cases, the AI is just a convenient label for layoffs that would have happened anyway. However, these reports completely underestimate the change happening before our eyes. On social media, people keep saying, "GenAI won't take your job; someone who uses it will." In the short term, that may be true, but it misses a much larger shift already underway.

  

I'm reading "Reshuffle: Who wins when AI restacks the knowledge economy" by Sangeet Paul Choudary, and it's becoming clear that many organizations will die because of these changes. (Sad.) Choudary uses two companies as early examples, both ethically challenged, Amazon and Shein. Amazon has reoriented itself entirely around the Prime Membership and the promise to get purchases to you in two days. Why buy elsewhere when Amazon has a good price and promises quick delivery? Shein has upended the fashion industry; they don't plan a year in advance, and they don't have layers of decision-making to reduce risk. They monitor social media, see what is trending, design an item that might fit that interest, produce a few hundred and see if it sells. If we ignore the ethics and environmental impact of both organizations (hard to do), they're examples of decentralized organizations that continually adapt their operations to how the world is working. Both are using AI to make decisions about how work flows through their entire business.

  

AI has upended much of retail, and now it is coming for knowledge work. In recent months, I've talked to people who have orgs that:

\- Require a separate Quality Assurance team

\- Have features in their Product Backlog that are years old

\- Require all decisions to be approved by several layers of managers and even end users

  

They've all "adopted" agile, but in the sense of making small improvements to an existing system. Not adopted in the sense of making fundamental and ongoing change.

  

Unfortunately, as the world of work changes, organizations that only want the Agile bumper sticker will struggle. To survive in this world, we're going to need to change not just the flow of work, but sometimes the work itself. True agility will be the minimum to survive in this mess. "Bumper Sticker Agile" won't be enough. Unlike Shein and Amazon, let's try to navigate with our ethics and humanity intact.

Clearly, I'm going to create a course and coaching to help in this area. Our survey is open to help us understand your needs. Certification requires a clear, stable target; most certifications are currently focused on improving prompt engineering and ethics. None is examining just how much this industry will change. In addition, these bodies are becoming more rigid in how material is presented, and that doesn't work in this landscape.

  

### Systems Thinking with GenAI: Solve Deep Team Problems

Somewhere in all this, I managed to write a blog post. For over 10yrs I've encouraged CSM and A-CSM students to engage in Systems Thinking to gain a deeper understanding of their challenges. Easy to describe, hard to do well, especially when you want to draw a Causal Loop Diagram. Enter GenAI. For once, I have something good to say about it. I've created a Claude Skill to coach people to use the tools without having to remember all of the pesky questions or know how create a funky diagram.
