---
subject: Radio silence and the AI tsunami
date: 2026-03-09
---

I've disappeared for the past two weeks; I needed to deal with some back-end issues. In particular, any of you who have used the Three Percent Better community have already received a notification that it is shutting down. This wasn't on my list of quarterly goals, and so it has soaked up a considerable amount of my time. Later in 2026, I will consider launching a new discussion platform with a narrower focus. In the meantime, I apologize for any inconvenience the shutdown causes.


## AI Tsunami
I can't go even a few minutes without hearing more noise about AI. I've survived every Gartner Hype Cycle since they were established, and this is noisest of them all. Between 1995 and 2001, the dot-com bubble was based on the promise that the internet would change everything. It did, just a lot later than Nortel, JDS Uniphase, Pets.com and WebVan expected it to pay off.


AI is a louder, noisier version of the dot-com bubble. Real changes are happening, and they will impact our world. We can't predict whether this is a bubble or the beginning of a new era. If it's a bubble, we will still end up with GenAI tools with capabilities similar to those we have today. If it’s not a bubble and companies like OpenAI and Anthropic succeed, then the size of the changes will be much larger.


No matter what happens, we need to adapt to the changes. The key question is, are these tools that augment our work or are corporations going to shrink?


Even if the tools don’t get better, they're already impacting our world. In software development, we already see more lines of code being written and [more bugs being introduced](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/ai-generated-code-quality-problems/). Yet, I also find teams that claim to be using AI and knocking it out of the park. Better quality than ever before.


As it currently stands, AI appears to be an amplifier. If you’re already doing well, AI seems to be a force multiplier. If your team/organization has challenges, AI will make them worse. Classic example: A team with either a bottleneck in either Decision-Making or Quality Assurance. They use AI to generate code, and now the bottleneck is worse. There are more decisions to make and a larger product surface area to test.


## Agile More Relevant Than Ever
Agile has always been about adapting to change. GenAI requires us to: look for the bottlenecks; run more process experiments; and run more product experiments. From a product management perspective, I can already see that these tools make it easier to run more product experiments. In my own experience, they make it easier to move my data from one product to another. Without good Quality and Product Market Fit, speed doesn’t matter.


There is a lot of work ahead of us to explore this new territory.


Pssst, I still write about Scrum: [Product Backlog Refinement Hell: 3 Problems and Solutions](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/product-backlog-refinement-hell-solutions/)


## Help Me Name What I'm doing
What I want to be is the person you trust to share both sides, the good and the bad. Someone mapping the territory as it actually is, not as vendors promise it will be.


I've been searching for a label that captures that middle ground. Three candidates:

🗺️ AI Cartographer - mapping the terrain, cliffs and all 

🏔️ AI Sherpa - trusted guide through difficult, uncertain territory 

📐 AI Surveyor - measuring what is really on the ground


Which one resonates with you? Tell me why you voted. Or suggest something better.

## What’s Next?
I'm off for the next two and a half weeks, exploring the Canary Islands (warmer than Ottawa in March) and trying to understand my place in this fast-changing world.


See you all in April.

Mark

## Mark's Reading Rabbit Hole
- [The 2028 global intelligence crisis](https://www.citriniresearch.com/p/2028gic) - **Not a prediction.** The authors use a thought experiment to explore the implications of GenAI for society. It is one possible outcome, not the most likely one. Read it to understand just how big the changes could be.

## Day 2 rebuilt — GenAI + Systems Thinking (horizontal death spiral)
You were right that the first pass paraphrased. I rebuilt it so nearly every clause is lifted verbatim from the post. Mapping is below so you can verify.

A senior architect is trapped in what he calls a "vicious death spiral." His Scrum Master decided to split the work: one team handles user stories while another manages technical integrations. Six sprints in, refinement and planning sessions routinely exceed eight hours. Stories arrive incomplete, missing critical integration details. Dependencies bounce between groups, estimates become guesswork, and team members mentally check out around hour five.

I used GenAI as a sparring partner to think this through with Systems Thinking. When I explained that everyone says the split is just more efficient, and that they're measuring how much work each person gets done, the model named it: a classic systems thinking trap called local optimization at the expense of global optimization. The organization is measuring output (how busy each specialist is) but not outcome (how quickly customer value flows through the system).

The most insightful element of the whole exchange: the system keeps trying to solve a structure problem with a process problem. The Scrum Master keeps extending sessions, believing more time will surface all hidden complexity, while the architect has watched the same story carry over three sprints because the slicing never works.

When your team keeps carrying the same story across sprints, ask whether you're solving a structure problem with a process problem.

## Definition of Ready — final (Option B text + Option A's closing question)
Most teams treat Definition of Ready as a checklist to enforce. I'd rather you hold it lightly.

If items frequently get stuck mid-Sprint because something was ill-understood, a Definition of Ready can help, but only cover the details that are actually causing problems right now. Instead of "all acceptance criteria", try "some or enough acceptance criteria have been found". Instead of "requires a mockup", try "features that need large UI changes check whether a mockup would help, preferring pencil sketches".

Then, as the team matures, check whether the Definition of Ready can be made thinner by reducing the number of elements in it. The failure mode to watch for is that it becomes a dumping ground for every little problem the team ever had. A lightweight check is a tool for good; a rigid gate that everything must 100% comply with is how you end up optimizing for looking productive instead of being useful.

Does your "Ready" gate reduce delay, or just hide it earlier in the process?

Here's a classic example. Take a team with a bottleneck in either decision-making or quality assurance. They use GenAI to generate code, and now the bottleneck is worse, because there are more decisions to make and a larger product surface area to test. Speed upstream just piles more work onto the part of the system that was already struggling.

This is why I keep saying Agile is more relevant than ever. Agile has always been about adapting to change, and GenAI requires us to look for the bottlenecks, run more process experiments, and run more product experiments. Without good quality and product-market fit, speed doesn't matter.

Between 1995 and 2001, that bubble was built on the promise that the internet would change everything. It did, just a lot later than Nortel, JDS Uniphase, Pets.com and WebVan expected it to pay off.
